In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta. Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and a manifest Book.﴾

We have spoken at length about these disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of the surahs. Here, "Ta Sin" are two letters of the alphabet, and they are pronounced as "Ta" and "Sin," because they are names of the letters. There is a difference between the name of a letter and what it denotes. Both the unlettered person and the educated person speak using letters. For example, one says: "Muhammad wrote the lesson." If you ask an unlettered person to spell these letters, he cannot, because he does not know the names of the letters, although he can pronounce what they denote. The educated person, however, says: "kaf, ta', ba'."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was unlettered and did not know the names of the letters. Therefore, these names come from God. For this reason, the matter is tawqifi (determined by divine revelation, not by human convention). So, the letters "Alif Lam Mim" at the beginning of al-Baqarah we pronounced by their letter names: "alif, lam, mim." But at the beginning of al-Inshirah, we said ﴿Alam nashrah laka sadrak? (Did We not expand your breast for you?)﴾ (al-Sharh), pronouncing them by the names of the letters themselves, so we say: "alam."

As for ﴿Tilka... ﴾ (al-Naml), it is a demonstrative referring to the verses that follow within this surah. We have said that the word "ayat" (verses/signs) has multiple meanings. It may refer to the cosmic signs, such as the sun and the moon: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon...﴾ (Fussilat 37).

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you mates from among yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them...﴾ (al-Rum 21). These cosmic signs are what draw our attention to the greatness of the Creator, may He be exalted, and His power.

"Ayat" also means the miracles accompanying the messengers, which establish the truth of their message from God. And "ayat" means the verses of the Qur'an carrying the rulings, and this is what is intended here: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an...﴾ (al-Naml).

God, may He be exalted, has said earlier: ﴿Alif Lam Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an﴾ (al-Hijr 1). Sometimes He says ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾ (al-Hijr) and sometimes ﴿and a manifest Book﴾ (al-Naml). He mentions "the Book" and joins "the Qur'an" to it, or He mentions "the Qur'an" and joins "the Book" to it, even though they are one and the same thing. How, then, can a thing be joined to itself?

They said: When a thing is joined to itself, know that this is to add a description of the thing. You say: "Zayd the poet, the orator, and the merchant came to me." Each attribute adds something from one aspect of the described person. So it is the Qur'an because it is recited in hearts, and it is itself the Book because it is written in lines. Both of them we sometimes call "the Qur'an" and sometimes "the Book," but the attribute makes a distinction present.

The meaning of ﴿manifest﴾ (al-Naml) is clear and evident, and it encompasses everything in the affairs of life and its movements, from commands and prohibitions, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ (al-An'am 38).

We have already related what happened with Imam Muhammad Abduh(1), may God have mercy on him, when he was in France. One of the orientalists asked him: "You say that the Qur'an encompasses everything. How many loaves are in an ardab of wheat?" The Imam summoned the baker and asked him, and he said: "Such and such." The orientalist said: "I want it from the Qur'an." The Imam said: "The Qur'an tells us: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ (al-Anbiya' 7)."

So it is as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ (al-An'am 38).

(1) He is Shaykh Muhammad Abduh ibn Hasan Khayr Allah of the Turkmani family, Mufti of Egypt, and one of the great figures of reform and renewal in Islam. He was born in the village of Shanra in al-Gharbiyya in Egypt (1849 CE). He grew up in Mahallat Nasr in al-Buhayra, held the office of judgeship, and died in Alexandria (1905 CE) at the age of 56, and he was buried in Cairo. He has many works. (Al-A'lam by al-Zirikli, 6/252).

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿A guidance and good news for the believers.﴾

Al-Huda (guidance) comes with two meanings: the meaning of indication (al-dalalah) to the path of goodness, and the meaning of assistance (al-ma'unah). In terms of indication, it is an indication for both the believer and the disbeliever alike, because it has pointed out and directed everyone. Then comes the guidance of assistance (hidayat al-ma'unah), in accordance with your following of the guidance of indication.

So whoever obeys Allah, believes in Him, and takes hold of His indication, it is as if the Truth, glorified is He, says to him: "You have entrusted Me with the movement of your life, and you have obeyed Me in My command and My prohibition, so I will lighten for you and make easy for you the matter of worship, and I will assist you in it." This is the guidance of assistance of which He said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Muhammad 17)

Likewise is the disbeliever who has not taken hold of the guidance of indication and guidance, and has chosen for himself another path, which Allah helps him to, and makes easy for him what he has striven for of disbelief. Therefore Allah sets a seal upon the hearts of the disbelievers, so that faith does not enter them and disbelief does not leave them.

But here, is the guidance (al-hidayah) the guidance of indication, or the guidance of assistance?

We say: it is the guidance of assistance, by the evidence of His saying, the Exalted, after it: ﴿and good news for the believers.﴾ (al-Naml). For they were not believers except because they were guided, and good news is only for the believers. So, then: it is assistance to the believers, by increasing them in guidance to the straight path, and to the gardens of bliss: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands; they say, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us; indeed You are Competent over all things."﴾ (al-Tahrim 8).

And if the guidance here meant the guidance of indication, which comes to both the believer and the disbeliever, it would have been good news and warning. But the verse ﴿and good news for the believers﴾ (al-Naml) determines that the meaning is the guidance of assistance and the guidance of good news.

The believers are the people of the creed of faith (iman), which is that you believe in the matter of the One Truth, the Chosen God, the Doer who possesses the attributes of perfection; you believe in it until it becomes a conviction in your soul, firm and unshakeable. Faith (iman) is belief in the heart, speech with the tongue, and action by the limbs. Merely uttering the tongue is not sufficient; there must be the fulfilment of the obligations and requirements of faith, the summit of which is the establishment of prayer (salah), the giving of zakah, the fasting of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage (hajj).

Prayer is a summons from God to His creation, a call from the Maker to the made. Your Lord summons you into His presence. How can a creation be presented to its maker five times every day, and yet we see someone who puts work before prayer, and when he hears the call says, "I have works and preoccupations"? Beware of thinking that prayer is a suspension of interests or a waste of time, for you are in the movement of your life amid the blessings of God, and in prayer you are with God.

Let us measure this matter—and to God belongs the highest likeness—if your father called you and you did not answer him, what would he do to you? So let your Lord not be less dear to you than your father. Your Lord calls you: "Allahu Akbar", meaning: Greater than work, and greater than everything that occupies you from answering His call.

In prayer we take a charge of faith that empowers us for the movement of our lives, just as if we took the car battery, for example, to the charging device; would you say that you had disabled the battery?

If we calculated the time that the five prayers take, we would find that it does not exceed one hour of the twenty-four hours, so do not begrudge yourself that hour to meet your Lord, to stand before Him and present yourself to Him. Then what the movement of life has corrupted in you will be set right, and He will give you the support, the help, and the charge of faith that propels you into a movement in harmony with life and with the universe around you.

If the engineer of a machine repairs it with a material thing, your Lord—Mighty and Majestic—is unseen, and He repairs you with the unseen, from where you do not know. For this reason prayer stands at the summit of the requirements of faith.

If prayer is for the reform of the self, then zakah is for the reform of wealth. Therefore you always find prayer paired with zakah in most verses. Wealth is the result of work, and work is a branch of time; prayer takes the time, while zakah takes the result of time. Zakah takes 2.5%, whereas prayer takes the time itself, that is, at a rate of 100%.

Nevertheless, we do not say that prayer has wasted time, for the charge you receive in prayer makes you accomplish in half an hour work that would take several hours, thus giving you blessing in time.

We have said before that the call "Allahu Akbar" means that meeting God is greater than anything that occupies you, however great you see it, because He—glory be to Him—is the giver of blessing and the giver of energy. And although work and striving across the earth are required, prayer in its time takes precedence.

When we consider the longest intervals between every two prayers, we find that they are from Fajr until Dhuhr, which is the suitable time for work, and from Isha until Fajr, which is the suitable time for sleep. Thus prayer organises our lives for us: from the Fajr prayer to the Dhuhr prayer is seven hours, which are the hours of work.

If the Islamic nation had held fast to its law and the method of its Lord, then after these seven hours that you spend at your work, you would be free after the Dhuhr prayer. But the specialisation that has come upon the movement of life has required that Dhuhr and even Asr come while people are still at their work.

As for those who delay the prayer beyond its time on the pretext that the interval between the two prayers is long—yes, the time is extended, but it is not permissible to delay the prayer. To clarify this matter, we say: suppose a wealthy person able to perform the hajj has not performed it; when does he sin?

He sins if long hope deceives him and then death overtakes him before he performs the hajj. But if his life is extended until he performs it, that obligation has fallen from him. Yet who guarantees for him that he will remain alive until he performs this duty?

For this reason it has come in a hadith: "Perform hajj before you are prevented from hajj" (1).

Likewise is the case with the time of prayer: it is extended, but who guarantees you its extension? Therefore the one who abandons prayer sins at the last moment of his life; if he remains until he prays, there is nothing upon him.

So do not make excuses with the length of the time, for the length of time was made by God for a wisdom, not so that we take it as a pretext to delay prayer beyond its time. The length of time between the prayers was made so that the sleeper may wake, or the forgetful may remember.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ (An-Naml).

So the verse gathers the whole matter of the believer: beginning with the creed and faith in God, then prayer, then zakah, which are the two practical demands, between two faiths: the first faith in God, and the other that he believes in the Hereafter, in recompense, the return, and the final destiny.

As for His saying ﴿they are certain﴾ (An-Naml), certainty (al-iqan) is judging a thing to be fixed without any imagined doubt. Therefore we have said that knowledge ('ilm) is that you know a established matter and say that it is true and provide proof for it.

We have said that certainty has degrees: the knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqin), the eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqin), and the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin). For example, when I tell you that I saw in a certain country a banana finger half a metre long, and you trust me and do not doubt me, this is the knowledge of certainty. If you see it, this is the eye of certainty. If you take it and go to cut it, for example, and distribute it to those present, this is the truth of certainty. This degree cannot have doubt seep into it.

Therefore, when the Prophet ﷺ asked the Companion al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari, "How have you woken up?" he said, "I have woken up a true believer in God." He said, "Every truth has a reality, so what is the reality of your faith?" He said, "My soul has turned away from this world, so its gold and its clay are alike to me, and it is as if I see the people of Paradise in Paradise enjoying themselves, and the people of the Fire in the Fire being punished." The Prophet ﷺ said to him, "You have known; then hold fast" (3).

And Imam ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, gives us a description of certainty in his saying: "Had the veil been lifted from me, I would not have increased in certainty, because I affirmed what God said, and my eye is not more truthful to me than God."

From this certainty is what we mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ (Al-Fil 1), although the Prophet ﷺ was born in that year and did not see that event. The meaning is: "Have you not seen," and it turned away from "do you not know" to "do you not see," to tell the Prophet ﷺ that God's report to you is more truthful than the sight of your eyes.

This is the commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 4:

These (the disbelievers in the Hereafter) stand in contrast to those who believe, establish the prayer and give the zakah (zakat), because Allah, blessed and exalted is He, presents a thing and its opposite so that we may make a comparison between opposites. Concerning these, He says: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appealing to them, so they wander in confusion.﴾ He did not deny them the establishment of the prayer and the giving of zakah. Why? Because they do not, in the first place, believe in Allah, nor in resurrection and reckoning. Had they known that they would return to Allah, they would have believed in Him and sent forward righteous deeds.

The meaning of ﴿We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾ is that those who do not believe in Allah, do not believe in the Hereafter, and do not fulfill the requirements of faith have no excuse. Indeed, when We presented faith and its requirements, We presented them well, attractively and enticingly, and We made them appealing to you.

So the prayer is a meeting between you and your Lord, expressing constant loyalty and giving you a charge of faith. And zakah secures you in your weakness and inability: We take from you while you are wealthy, so that We may give to you if poverty befalls you. And when We forbade you from lying, We forbade all people from lying to you; and when We warned you against bribery, We said to others: Do not consume his property without right... etc.

Thus We explained the obligations, clarified their wisdom, and made them beloved to you.

Or the meaning may be: We made appealing to them the deeds they were doing; then, when Allah knew of their love for misguidance and deviation, He sealed their hearts. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him so that he sees it as good...﴾ (Fatir 35:8)

But who is it that made it appealing to them? ﴿Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾ (al-Nahl 16:63). So the beautifying comes once from Satan, once with an unidentified agent, and once Allah made it appealing to them.

From Allah's beautifying is His saying concerning Pharaoh: ﴿And Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the worldly life, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way..."﴾ (Yunus 10:88). So when Allah gave them blessings, they were tested by them.

Iblis is a creation of Allah, and He made for him offspring who dominate people and lead them astray. This is only for the sake of choice, so that He may see who will stand at these doors. Thus, Allah, blessed and exalted, has not placed barriers against disobedience, but has placed incentives toward obedience. The matter rests with you: if I see you inclining toward something and loving it, I will assist you in it.

Whoever dies over his loss, such as a man of honour, or a woman whose child dies, and she remains grieving over him, troubling her life and the lives of those around her – and would that this benefited or returned the dead – we say to one who receives Allah's decree with such anger: Indeed your Lord, when He knows that you have become accustomed to sorrow and have come to love it, while He is the Lord, must give you what you seek and open for you every day one of its doors.

So: whoever is exposed to such a trial should receive it with contentment and close the door of grief, not leaving it ajar.

From beautifying is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase for him his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We give him from it, but he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾ (al-Shura 42:20)

The meaning of ﴿they wander blindly﴾ (يعمهون, al-Naml 27:4) is that they are bewildered and agitated, not knowing where they are going.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 5:

"Ay" (meaning): the evil punishment. This refers to the Hereafter. In addition to what befell them of slaughter at Badr and a defeat that broke their strength, the matter did not end at this limit; rather, there is another loss in the Hereafter: ﴿And in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾ (al-Naml).

"Al-akhsar" is an intensive form of "al-khusran" (loss). He did not say "khasir" but "akhsar," because he has lost the bliss, since he did not send forth any righteous deed in the world. Would that he had remained without bliss and been left in his state; rather, the punishment that distresses him comes upon him. Therefore, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the greatest losers﴾ (al-Naml), because they did not enter Paradise, and this is a loss. Then they are in the Fire, and this is another loss.

This means: these matters and affairs come to you only from Allah, the All-Wise, the All-Knowing, who places each thing in its proper measure and its proper place. So whether He rewards the doer of good or punishes the doer of evil, each is in its place, and He, glorified is He, is the All-Knowing of what He assigns as recompense for good deeds and for evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 7:

The Truthful Lord (al-Haqq, subhanahu) relates to us the story of Musa (peace be upon him):

﴿When Musa said to his family, "I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾

We have only recently mentioned a portion of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in Surah al-Shu'ara', and here the context returns to it once more. Why? Because the call of Musa (peace be upon him) occupied a great portion of the Noble Qur'an, for they followed their prophets and opposed them stubbornly, so that much was said about them.

It is strange that they boast of the great number of their prophets, while they do not know that this is counted against them, not for them. A prophet does not come except when his people are wretched, and the Children of Israel were in such misguidance and obstinacy that one messenger was not enough for them; they needed a "consultation" (consulto) of prophets. They regard this as a source of pride, while it is a deficiency and a blame.

As for the repetition of the story of the Children of Israel and Musa (peace be upon him) many times in the Qur'an, it is because the Qur'an does not narrate a "tale" (hadduta), nor does it mention events in order to record history. Rather, it brings from the story what suits the place of lesson and of strengthening the heart of the Messenger of Allah: ﴿And all that We relate to you of the news of the messengers is that by which We make firm your heart...﴾ (Hud: 120). This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encountered in the journey of the call many hardships and difficulties, and he needed consolation(1) and strengthening. So his Lord brings him a particular snapshot, but does not present the story in full. This is not incapacity—far be it from Allah—to present the story in full at once.

Indeed, He (subhanahu) presented the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him) in full, from alif to ya', in the form of a well-woven story, in the highest form of narrative art. Yet, apart from this story, no mention of Our Master Yusuf (peace be upon him) came except in two places:

The first: in Surah al-An'am: ﴿And of his offspring, Dawud and Sulayman and Ayyub and Yusuf...﴾ (al-An'am: 84).

The other: in Surah Ghafir: ﴿And certainly Yusuf came to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you, until when he died you said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger..."﴾ (Ghafir: 34).

Thus, the appearance of the story in different, scattered snapshots is not an incapacity to present it complete in one context; had He done so, the strengthening would have been only once.

Here the Truthful Lord says: ﴿When Musa said to his family, "I have perceived a fire..."﴾ (al-Naml: 7), and in another place He says: ﴿He said to his family, "Stay here, I have perceived a fire..."﴾ (al-Qasas: 29). In this verse there is a new addition not present in the first.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term(2) and set out with his family, he perceived from the side of the mount a fire...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29), i.e., he perceived it for himself. Whereas in the two previous verses he reports that he perceived a fire. So each verse is in a situation, and there is no repetition in the matter, as some imagine.

Musa (peace be upon him) travels with his family along this rugged road, and darkness descends upon him, and he can no longer see the way. So he says to his wife: ﴿I have perceived a fire...﴾ (al-Naml: 7), meaning: I will go to take a brand from it, so that they may be guided by it, or warm themselves by it.

It is natural that his wife objects to him: how can you leave me alone in this desolate place? So he says to her: ﴿Stay...I have perceived a fire...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29), meaning: remain here resting, and I will be the one who goes, for perhaps you would be exposed to dangers if you were far from them. Thus these are new situations called for by the circumstances, not repetition.

Likewise we find a natural difference in His saying: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it some news...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29) and His saying: ﴿I will bring you from it some news...﴾ (al-Naml: 7).

The first, ﴿Perhaps...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29), contains hope, because he is approaching something about which he is in doubt and is not certain, and in this state he is truthful with the thoughts of his own soul before something absent from him. But when he became certain, he said ﴿I will bring you...﴾ (al-Naml: 7) with the certainty(3).

In this matter he said once: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it some news or a brand...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29), and here he said: ﴿I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves(4).﴾ (al-Naml: 7).

This is because he does not know, when he reaches the fire, whether he will find it blazing with a tongue of flame from which he can take a kindled brand, or find that it has subsided and nothing remains of it but a jadhwa, which is a glowing piece like charcoal, for example. So every repetition here has its place and its meaning, and adds something new to the context of the story. It is a completion of snapshots that come scattered according to the intended purpose of lesson and strengthening.

As for the phrase ﴿li-ahlihi﴾ (to his family) (al-Naml: 7), they said it means a group, as evidenced by His saying to them ﴿Stay...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29). He was with his wife, and with him were also some shepherds or servants. A person among us needs many things that require plurality: this one cooks the food, this one is for cleanliness, this one for ironing clothes... etc.

But there is one thing that no one can fulfil for you except your wife: offspring and marital intimacy. Likewise the wife alone can perform all these tasks; so she suffices in place of all the family, and we may say that with him there was none but his wife.

This is common in our language: a man says "the group" or "my group" or "my family," meaning his wife, and in this there is an honouring by the husband of his wife's station.

As for the meaning of ﴿ānastu﴾ (I have perceived) (al-Naml: 7): ānasa means he felt and sensed something that made him at ease and reassured him, and its opposite is tawajjus, i.e., he felt and sensed something he concealed, and from it His saying, exalted is He, also concerning Musa: ﴿So Musa felt fear within himself. We said, "Fear not; indeed, you are the superior"﴾ (Ta-Ha: 67-68).

1 Salani min hammi, tasliyatan wa aslani: i.e., he removed it from me. Insalat 'anni al-hamm wa tasalla bi-ma'na: i.e., it was uncovered. Abu Zayd said: the meaning of salawtu is when he forgot its mention and became oblivious to it. (Lisan al-'Arab, root: s-l-y)

2 I.e., the term which Shu'ayb set for him in return for marrying his daughter, when he said: ﴿Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years; but if you complete ten, it is from you...﴾ (al-Qasas: 27). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/387): "Musa fulfilled the better and more complete of the two terms, and the most pure and perfect."

(305): "If you say: how does He say here ﴿sa-ātīkum...﴾ (al-Naml: 7), and in ﴿la'allī ātīkum...﴾ (al-Qasas: 29), while one of them is definite and the other is hopeful, and the matter is one? I say: the one who hopes, when his hope grows strong, may say: I will do such-and-such, and it will be such-and-such, while permitting the possibility of not being decided."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 27, verse 8:

Meaning: he came to the fire, and ﴿he was called out to...﴾ (An-Naml 8). The nida' (calling) is a request for attention, as you say, "O so-and-so!" and he comes to you and you tell him what you want. So the calling in the Almighty's saying ﴿O Musa﴾ (Ta-Ha 11) is a nida', and ﴿Indeed, I am Allah...﴾ (Ta-Ha 14) is an address and an informing.

But what is the meaning of ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it...﴾ (An-Naml 8), and he did not say "O Musa"? So there is no nida' here. They said: mere address (khitab) is intended here as nida', because as long as He is addressing him, it is as if He is calling him. An example of this is the Almighty's saying: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true..."﴾ (Al-A'raf 44). Here the address is mentioned directly without a nida', because the nida' is here understood and known from the context of the speech. Also from this is: ﴿And the companions of the heights will call out to men whom they will recognize by their marks, saying, "Your gathering has not availed you, nor what you used to be arrogant about."﴾ (Al-A'raf 48).

Also from this is: ﴿So he called to her from below her, "Do not grieve..."﴾ (Maryam 24). Here He made the address itself the nida'.

As for His saying ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it...﴾ (An-Naml 8): the word buurika (blessed) does not suit fire, because fire burns. And since He said ﴿blessed is whoever is in the fire...﴾ (An-Naml 8), there must be a creation within the fire that is not burned and on which the fire has no effect. Who, then, are those on whom the fire has no effect? They are the angels(1).

Musa (peace be upon him) saw a wondrous scene: he saw the fire blazing on a branch of the tree, while the fire increased and the branch increased in greenness. The fire did not burn the greenness, and the greenness's moisture and water did not extinguish the fire(2). Who can control such a matter? Therefore, after it He said: ﴿Glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (An-Naml 8).

So in such a situation, beware of saying "How?" Rather, declare Allah far above your own dispositions. This is wondrous and cannot be imagined from your perspective, whereas with Allah it is a simple matter.

We have seen a similar miracle in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when his Lord saved him from the fire. The purpose of that event was not merely the rescue of Ibrahim. Had Allah wished only to save him, they would not have been able to seize him, or He would have extinguished the fire they kindled with a rain-laden cloud; there were many possible means for the rescue of our master Ibrahim.

But Allah the Exalted willed that they should seize him, cast him into the fire in its state of blazing and glowing, and that they themselves should throw him into it while they saw all of this with their own eyes, and then the fire did not harm him. It is as if He is saying to them: "I want to save him from the fire, despite the strength of your means of burning him. I am the Creator of the fire and the One who gave it the property of burning, and it is obedient to My command. I say to it, 'Be coolness and safety,' and it becomes so. The matter is not a law and a rule governing the universe; rather, it is My sustaining power (qayyumiyyah) over My creation."

So: what Musa (peace be upon him) saw of the fire blazing in the greenness of the tree is a wondrous matter to you, but it is not wondrous to One who possesses the freedom of power that breaks through laws.

The passive form in ﴿buurika﴾ (blessed) (An-Naml 8) means that Allah the Exalted is the One who blesses, and this is a matter no one can do except Allah. ﴿Whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾ (An-Naml 8) may refer to the angels, or: the tree itself is blessed, because it is not burned; or the fire is blessed, because it is not extinguished.

In another place He widens the circle of blessing, saying: ﴿from the blessed spot in the tree...﴾ (Al-Qasas 30).

(1) Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the Almighty's saying ﴿when he came to it, he was called out to, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire..."﴾ (An-Naml 8): it means Tabaraka wa Ta'ala Himself; the light of the Lord of the worlds was in the tree. ﴿And whoever is around it﴾ (An-Naml 8) means the angels. Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/341).

(2) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/356): "When he came to it and saw a tremendous, great sight, arriving at it while the fire was blazing in a green tree, the fire increasing only in its kindling and the tree increasing only in greenness and freshness. Then he raised his head and saw its light connected to the horizon of the sky. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it was not fire, but light that was blazing." 

(3) That is: from the direction of the tree. It was said: it was a tree of 'ulayq (a thorny shrub). It was said: samurah (a type of acacia). It was said: 'awsaj (boxthorn), and from it was Musa's staff, as al-Zamakhshari mentioned. When 'awsaj grows large it is called gharqad. (al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 7/5168.)

Then the Truthful Lord addresses Moses:

﴿O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [27:9]

The call comes here in its true form, with the vocative particle and the one being addressed: ﴿innahu ana Allah...﴾ [27:9] (an-Naml). This is the principle: since I am Allah, do not be astonished at what you see, and when you hear one speaking to you without seeing a speaker of your own kind, do not be amazed or startled.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 27, verse 10:

We notice here details and events that this verse does not mention, which are mentioned in another place in His saying: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses? He said, "It is my staff; I lean on it and beat down [leaves] for my sheep, and I have in it other uses."﴾ (Ta-Ha)

Courtesy (adab) requires that the answer be in proportion to the question. But Moses, peace be upon him, wished to prolong the intimacy with God and remain in His presence, the Exalted. When Moses sensed that he had lingered in this station, he was brief, and said: ﴿and I have in it other uses﴾ (Ta-Ha). So the staff has many other functions in his life.

Here He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And throw down your staff...﴾ (An-Naml 10). That is: if the staff is, for you, of this simplicity, and this is its function for you, then it has for Me another function. So look at its function with Me, and at what you do not know about it.

﴿And throw down your staff...﴾ (An-Naml 10). So when Moses threw down his staff, he saw it ﴿moving as if it were a snake...﴾ (An-Naml 10). That is: a serpent that slithers and moves. What is remarkable is that it did not transform into something of its own kind. The staff is a piece of wood, a branch that was a shoot on a tree; its kind is vegetation. When it was cut and dried, it became inert matter. Had it returned to the vegetative state, that is, to the nearer kind, and turned green, it would have been wondrous.

But the Truth, blessed and exalted, transferred it to another kind, to the animal kingdom. This is a great leap that inspires astonishment and even fear, especially when it is ﴿moving as if it were a snake...﴾ (An-Naml 10), that is, moving rapidly here and there.

It is natural for Moses' disposition, on seeing the staff in his hand in this form, to become afraid and agitated: ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself. We said, "Fear not; indeed, you are the superior"﴾ (Ta-Ha 67–68).

The meaning of ﴿the superior﴾ (Ta-Ha 68) is an indication that He is preparing him for a great mission, and that this staff will have a role against the opponents, and he will triumph over them and be the superior one. When you follow the various scenes of this story, you find it at one time a (jann), at another a (ḥayya, serpent), and at another a (thu'bān, large snake); all of these are states of one thing. The jann is the young of the thu'bān and has a lightness of movement that the thu'bān lacks, while the ḥayya is the large thu'bān.

His saying: ﴿And he turned back, retreating, and did not return...﴾ (An-Naml 10). That is: he turned away from it and presented his back to it. ﴿And did not return...﴾ (An-Naml 10). We say: so-and-so yuʿaqqib, meaning he turns on his heel and returns; the meaning is that he turned away from it and did not come back to it. Therefore his Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, called to him: ﴿O Moses, fear not; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ (An-Naml 10).

We notice here two calls, in which Moses, peace be upon him, is named as the one addressed, and they seem to be a compensation for the earlier call in which he was addressed with the announcement: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it...﴾ (An-Naml 8).

The reason for not fearing ﴿fear not...﴾ (An-Naml 10) is to let him know that he will be obliged to enter a battle, so let him be steadfast of heart and not fear, because he is not going to fight a single person, but a host of magicians gathered from every region of the land. He had already been told: ﴿indeed, you are the superior﴾ (Ta-Ha 68), so that this multitude would not terrify him.

Here He said: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ (An-Naml 10). The meaning: do not fear, for it is I who sent you, and it is I who take charge of your protection and support, as the Truth, glory be to Him, said in another place:

﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers, that they would indeed be helped, and that Our soldiers would indeed be the victors﴾ (As-Saffat 171–173).

So you are excused for fear if you were far from Me, but how so, when you are in My vicinity and I am with you, and here I am addressing you?

But Moses' throwing of the staff this time was merely a trial run (berova) so that he would become accustomed to this matter and at ease with it, and it would become for him a training and exercise. So when he performed this act before Pharaoh and the magicians, he performed it with confidence, steadfastness, and certainty of the possibility of the staff turning into a serpent.

After that comes a sign establishing that the domain of obligation (taklif) applies to humans, even to the messengers; the messengers too are obligated, and every obligated person may obey or disobey. But the messengers are protected from sin (ma'sum). As for Moses, peace be upon him, he had a particular incident when he struck the man and he fell dead. So he said: ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara 14).

In another place He specifies this sin: ﴿I killed a man among them, so I fear they will kill me﴾ (Al-Qasas 33).

We place this story before us so that we may understand:

﴿Except for one who has done wrong and then substituted good after evil — indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

So then: the exception here is from the Almighty's saying ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ (An-Naml). It makes an exception from that: ﴿Except for one who has done wrong and then substituted good after evil...﴾ (An-Naml).

It is as if He, may He be exalted, is alluding by this to the particular incident concerning Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Except for one who has done wrong...﴾ (An-Naml), that is, when he killed the Copt(1). But Musa, peace be upon him, acknowledged his sin and asked his Lord for forgiveness, saying: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me,﴾ and He forgave him... (Al-Qasas, 16).

And there is no objection to anyone after Allah, may He be exalted, forgives the sinner(2); for after he has done wrong ﴿then substituted good after evil...﴾ (An-Naml), meaning: he performed a good deed after the sin he had committed ﴿indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (An-Naml).

(1) The Copt is the Egyptian, a man of the city belonging to Pharaoh, and it is not meant to be the Christian. Musa came many generations before Isa, and between them there were many prophets and messengers.
(2) Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5043): "When someone close to the ruler commits an offence, then even if that offence is forgiven him, the effect of that offence remains; and as long as the effect and the suspicion persist, fear exists—not fear of punishment, but fear of the greatness (of the ruler). The one accused before the sultan finds in the accusation a lingering unease that leads to clouding the clarity of trust. Musa, peace be upon him, had committed that offence against that Pharaonic man, then he sought forgiveness and confessed to wronging himself, and then he was forgiven."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without harm, among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [27:12]

This is another sign and a new miracle. He mentioned it elsewhere, saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom...﴾ [28:32]

So what is the difference between "adkhil yadaka" (insert your hand) and "usluk yadaka" (pass your hand)? They said: because at the moment he puts his hand into his bosom, meaning the opening of the shirt, if the opening of the shirt is open, he inserts his hand easily, and this is called (idkhal, insertion).

But if it is closed (having buttons, for example), he needs to pass his hand (uslik yadahu), meaning he inserts it gently and makes room for it. We say: salaka al-shay' (he passed the thing), meaning: he inserted it gently and softly, and from this comes al-silk al-raqiq (the fine thread) when you insert it into something.

When we hear the word al-jayb (the bosom/pocket), we find it has a customary meaning among people and a linguistic meaning. Its meaning in the language is the upper opening of the shirt, which is at the neck. Its customary meaning is an opening inside the garment in which a person places his money. They say (jayb), and the common people have an excuse in that, because they have been forced to keep their money inside their clothes so that it is not visible, and perhaps pickpockets and villains steal it from them.

Peasants in the countryside still put the pocket in the inner (sudayri) vest. Therefore we have heard, for example, the street performer say—to move people's hearts toward him—"May God bless whoever puts his hand in his pocket," meaning: may God bless the one who gives me a pound.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿it will come out white, without harm...﴾ [27:12], that is: and when you withdraw it, it comes out bright and radiant. It is known that Moses, peace be upon him, was dark-complexioned, meaning swarthy, so when they saw his color change to whiteness, they might have said that this is an illness like leprosy, for example.

Therefore God removed this suspicion by His saying: ﴿without harm...﴾ [27:12], meaning without illness, ﴿among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people...﴾ [27:12], so that Moses, peace be upon him, would know that this sign is one of nine other signs by which God strengthens him before his enemy Pharaoh and his people.

These nine are: the staff, which has two functions: that it turns into a serpent before the magicians, and that it strikes the sea before his army when Pharaoh and his soldiers attack him. Then the hand. Then two: the drought and the loss of fruits, in His saying: ﴿And We seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits...﴾ [7:130]. Then: the flood, the locusts, the lice(1), the frogs, and the blood. These are the nine signs that established Moses before Pharaoh and his people. Was Moses sent to Pharaoh specifically? No, he was sent to the Children of Israel, but he wanted to persuade Pharaoh that he was sent from God, so that he would not stand between him and them. The matter of calling Pharaoh to faith in God came incidentally within the events of the story; it is not the foundation of Moses's mission, peace be upon him.

The meaning of ﴿Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people﴾ [27:12] is an indication that a person, even if he is a disbeliever who has left obedience to God, still originates from believing loins, and what is meant is the first faith in Adam, peace be upon him, and in his offspring after him. But they transgressed, that is, they went out of the covering of responsibility that wraps the movement of their lives, as we say: "fasaqat al-rutbah" (the fresh date fruit left its skin), meaning it came out of its covering. Likewise, a person transgresses, that is, he goes out of the sphere of responsibility that protects him.

(1) Lice: small insects that harm crops and annoy people. (Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/134). Ibn Manzur said in al-Lisan, entry "qaml": "Qaml: small gnats and flies. It was said: it is the fly that has no wings. Ibn al-Sikkit said: qaml is something that falls on crops, not locusts, which eats the ear of grain while still tender before it emerges, so the crop grows tall with no ear. Al-Azhari said: this is the correct view."

Then the Almighty says:

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clear to see, they said: "This is evident magic."﴾

"Signs" (āyāt): the miracles that establish the truth of the Messenger. The word "mubṣirah" (clear, making things visible) is in the form of a passive participle (ism al-maf'ūl), so how can it be in the form of an active participle (ism al-fā'il)? This is a matter we have only recently come to understand. From ancient times, among the Greeks and the earlier civilizations, people thought that seeing things with the eye occurs by a ray that emerges from the eye toward the visible object, until the Muslim scholar Ibn al-Haytham (al-Ḥasan ibn al-Haytham) came to refute this theory and to state the opposite of it.

So seeing is accomplished by a ray emerging from the visible object to the eye, as evidence that we do not see an object if it is in darkness while we are in light; but if the object is in light and you are in darkness, you can see it.

Therefore, it is as if the signs themselves are the ones that make things visible, because they are the ones that send out the rays that cause sight. Or: the signs are so clear that it is as if they insist that people see and reflect, so that they are, in terms of the truths, more perceptive ("abṣar") than them.

Note on "mubṣirah": that is, clear, evident, manifest. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/357). Al-Jawhari said: mubṣirah means luminous (muḍī'ah). Abu Ishaq said: the meaning of mubṣirah is that it makes them see, i.e., it makes things clear to them. Al-Akhfash said: it makes them see, i.e., we make them perceptive (baṣīrūn). (Lisan al-Arab, root b-ṣ-r).

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ [27:14]

﴿And they denied....﴾ [27:14] i.e., with the tongue. ﴿...them...﴾ [27:14] the signs. ﴿...though their souls were convinced...﴾ [27:14] of them, in belief. So the matter is one of obstinacy and contentiousness in dispute. Therefore He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿wrongdoing and arrogance...﴾ [27:14] i.e., haughtiness towards the truth. ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾ [27:14] And He left their end unspecified in order to magnify its matter and make it fearful.

Then he leaves the story of Moses with Pharaoh and what happened in it, for another occasion that requires a different kind of reinforcement, and moves on to another story in the procession of the prophets, which likewise contains occasions for lessons and reinforcement:

﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to David and Solomon, and they said: "All praise is for Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ (15)

You may ask: Allah gave David and Solomon, peace be upon them, many blessings besides knowledge. He made iron soft for David, and gave Solomon a kingdom that should not belong to anyone after him, subjected the wind and the jinn to him, and taught him the speech of the birds... etc. Yet He did not single them out for favour except with knowledge, which is the method of the religion?

They said: Because knowledge is the true blessing that the believer should rejoice in, not kingship, nor wealth, nor the whole world. They did not give weight to any of these things. Therefore they praised Allah for giving them knowledge, because it is the blessing that all creation needs, whereas kingship, status, or the subjection of the universe to one's service can be dispensed with by a person.

When Imam Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) exiled Abu Dhar, because he used to speak about wealth, its dangers, buildings, and worldly matters, they banished him to al-Rabadha so that he would not stir up strife. But before he left, he passed by Imam Ali so that he would intercede for him to be pardoned. Imam Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) did not want to intervene in this matter, lest it be said that Ali had set Abu Dhar against the people of this world to oppose and attack them. So he said to him: "O Abu Dhar, you have become angry for the sake of Allah, so flee from those for whose sake you became angry. The people feared you for their worldly life and their kingship, and you feared them for your religion. So flee with what you feared for, meaning: flee with your religion, and leave what they feared for you. How much they need what you have withheld from them, and how independent you are of what they have withheld from you."(1)

In this way Imam Ali removed this difficulty and showed the importance of knowledge and the method of Allah, such that the Muslim cannot do without it in any circumstance and cannot live without it, and through it he attains a lofty, enduring life in the hereafter, whereas a person can live without wealth and without kingship.

For this reason, the caliph of the Muslims sent to our master Ja'far al-Sadiq: "O son of the daughter of Muhammad (ﷺ), why do you not visit us as other people do?" That is: why do you not come to us, sit with us, and converse with us? He replied: "I have nothing of this world that you could fear for me," meaning: I have no wealth that you could confiscate, "and you have nothing of the hereafter that I could hope for from you." This is the very same reasoning that Imam Ali expressed.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said: All praise is for Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants.﴾ (al-Naml, 15). So the praise here is for the blessing of knowledge and the preservation of Allah's method. In the verse there is a manifestation of the courtesy of prophethood, in that they said ﴿has favoured us over many of His believing servants﴾ (al-Naml, 15). It is as though there were others better than them, and the favouring is not a restriction upon them; this is from the humility of these two, peace be upon them.

1 Ibn al-Jawzi cited in Sifat al-Safwa (1/303): "al-Bukhari related in his Afrad from the hadith of Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: I passed by al-Rabadha and said to Abu Dhar: What brought you here? He said: I was in Syria and I disagreed with Mu'awiya over this verse, ﴿Those who hoard gold and silver...﴾ (al-Tawba, 34). He said: It was revealed concerning the People of the Book. I said: It concerns us and them. So he wrote complaining about me to Uthman. Uthman wrote: Come to Medina. I came, and people gathered around me as if they had not seen me before. This was mentioned to Uthman, and he said: If you wish, withdraw and be nearby. That is what brought me to this place." This incident took place during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, and Abu Dhar died during Uthman's time. This does not preclude that Abu Dhar consulted Ali ibn Abi Talib, since he was not yet caliph.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 16:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And Solomon inherited from David. And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of all things. Indeed, this is evident bounty."﴾ [16]

The words of the Exalted, ﴿And Solomon inherited from David... [16]﴾ (al-Naml). That is: prophethood and the bearing of the method (al-manhaj) remained in him, not kingship, because the prophets are not inherited, as in the noble hadith: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity."(1)

This shows that Solomon came after David, yet he inherited prophethood from him, even though they were contemporaries, as is evident from the Exalted's words in another place: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field when the sheep of a people had grazed in it at night, and We were witness to their judgment.﴾ (al-Anbiya) [78](2)

Thus Solomon was with David in this judgment and in knowledge, but the Truth, glorified is He, made knowledge into degrees, as is evident from His saying: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon...﴾ (al-Anbiya) [79], even though his father was present, and he (David) had ruled in the case that the owner of the field should take the sheep that had eaten it.

When they left David's presence, Solomon asked them about his father's ruling. They informed him of what he had said, and Solomon said: "Rather, the owner of the field should take the sheep to benefit from them, and the owner of the sheep should take the field and restore it until it returns to what it was; then the owner of the sheep takes his sheep and the owner of the field takes his field."(3)

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, gives us this example with a prophet and his father, not with two distant, differing prophets. This points to the fact that the right of fatherhood did not prevent Solomon from differing with his father in the ruling, because God the Exalted said of them both: ﴿And to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge...﴾ (al-Anbiya) [79]. Each of them judged according to the requirement of the knowledge that God had granted him.

From this incident we derive the legitimacy of appeal and review (al-isti'naf wa al-naqd) in court rulings. When the appellate judge amends the ruling of the primary judge, this is not considered an attack upon it; rather, each of them ruled on the basis of his knowledge, and on the evidence and facts available to him, and perhaps the second judge perceived what the first judge had not perceived.

Therefore ﴿And Solomon inherited from David... [16]﴾ (al-Naml) does not mean that he came after him; rather, they were contemporaries, and he inherited from him in knowledge, prophethood and wisdom, not in kingship and wealth, because God the Exalted wills that the Messenger, in his message and his conveying from God, be far removed from any benefit that might come to him or to his offspring.

For this reason, the poor among the Prophet's family (ﷺ) did not take from the zakat of the believers. But where is this wise legislation from what happens now among rulers, officials and officeholders who favor their relatives and plunder the lands for their sake?

﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds... [16]﴾ (al-Naml). Birds have a speech and a language, because, as the Exalted said: ﴿And there is no creature in the earth, nor bird that flies with its wings, but that they are communities like you...﴾ (al-An'am) [38]. Now, with the advancement of knowledge, scholars speak of a language of ants, a language of bees, a language of fish... etc.

These creatures understand one another in their languages with an instinctive precision of understanding, but we do not understand this speech. The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, teaches us: ﴿And there is not a thing but exalts His praise, but you do not understand their glorification...﴾ (al-Isra') [44]. If you say, as some have said, that it is a glorification of indication (dalala), not speech or utterance, we say: since God the Exalted said ﴿but you do not understand their glorification...﴾ (al-Isra') [44], it must be speech and discourse, but you do not understand it.

Linguists say that articulate speech is specific to humans, while what animals and birds produce are sounds they make at all times, such as the meowing of a cat, the barking of a dog, the lowing of cattle and the croaking of frogs. But these sounds have meaning: the cat's "naw-naw" when hungry is other than its "nawna" when afraid.

Thus they express themselves, but we do not know these expressions, and how could we, when we humans do not know each other's languages, because we have not learned them. Language is a social necessity upon which we agree, that is, we agree that this word means such-and-such; when you utter it I understand you, and when I utter it you understand me.

Language is the daughter of hearing: the word you hear you can pronounce, and the word you have not heard you cannot pronounce, even if it is an Arabic word from your language, and you do not know its meaning either. If I said to you: "innama al-hayzabun wal-dardabis wal-takha wal-nakhalih wal-'aslabis," you would certainly not know a meaning for this, because we have not agreed upon its meaning.

A child raised in an Arabic environment speaks Arabic because he has heard it, and does not speak English, for example, because he has not heard it. Were that same child placed in an English environment, he would speak English, because language is not tied to race or blood; language is hearing.

The meaning of ﴿and we have been given of all things... [16]﴾ (al-Naml) is: of blessings in the absolute sense. Shortly we will hear this very phrase said by the hoopoe concerning the Queen of Sheba: ﴿and she has been given of all things...﴾ (al-Naml) [23]. Thus she is like him in what suits such kings, not in prophethood and bearing the method. ﴿Indeed, this is evident bounty [16]﴾ (al-Naml): the bounty that encompasses all virtues.

(1) A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4033), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (1757), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity."
(2) Nafashat al-ghanam: the sheep spread out in pasture without a shepherd or controller. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/279). Ibn Manzur said in (Lisan al-Arab, root n-f-sh): "The camels and sheep spread out at night and grazed; this does not happen by day, and some have specified its use for sheep entering a field of crops."
(3) Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/186) from Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 17:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And for Solomon were gathered his hosts of the jinn and the men and the birds, and they were kept in ranks.﴾ [17]

"Hushiru" (ḥushirū): they were gathered from every place. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And send into the cities summoners.﴾ [36] (al-Shu'ara'). Al-hashr (gathering) is the gathering of people for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection.

Gathering is called "jam'" (assembly) because you gather people from scattered places into one place, until they are crowded and pressed together. This is the meaning of hashr as commonly understood among us; we say: "nahshuruhum 'ala ba'd" (we gather them upon one another).

The meaning of ﴿fahum yuza'un﴾ [17] (al-Naml) is: they are held back (yumna'un). From it is his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed God restrains with the authority what He does not restrain with the Qur'an" (inna Allaha layuza'u bi-l-sultan ma la yuza'u bi-l-Qur'an). That is: authority, power and force restrain what the Qur'an cannot restrain, because they (people) consider the Resurrection and the punishment far off, whereas authority is a present and immediate deterrent.

But, from what are they held back while they are at the place of gathering before Solomon? They said [1]: they are held back from one of them preceding another to Solomon; rather, we hold them back until the last of them arrives, and they enter upon him all together at one time, and in that is the creation of balance among the whole subject people.

We have been told that the Prophet (ﷺ) had among his characteristics that when he sat in a gathering, his glances and his eye were distributed over all those sitting, so that he would treat them equally, and would not look at one more than another [2], nor distinguish any of them over another, so that none of them would think that the Prophet preferred him over others.

The Prophet (ﷺ) would not draw near except to the people of virtue and piety, those who were known not to exploit this status to gain authority among people. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) would not settle places (for individuals) and forbade that [3], unlike what we see now from some worshippers who place a prayer mat, for example, in the first row, occupying the place with it, then go off to attend to their needs, and return when the mosque is full, so they step over people's necks to reach a place at the front, and it is not their place with God.

So God, exalted is He, has distributed places according to order of arrival; your coming early to the House of God gives you the reward of the first row even if you pray in the last row. Not settling places spreads familiarity among people, removes distinctions, and helps acquaintance; every prayer in which you stand beside a new person, you get to know them and their circumstances.

But in light of this meaning of the root (w-z-' / waza'a), how do we understand His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord, enable me that I may be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me...﴾ [19] (al-Naml)?

"Awza'ni" here means: enable me and restrain me from heedlessness of Your favour, so that I remain thankful to You.

[1] Ibn 'Abbas said something similar: he placed over each category of them wardens (wazaʿa) who turn the first of them back toward the last, lest they advance in the march as kings do. Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/347) and attributed to Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

[2] Among the courtesies of prophethood: no one would take the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) hand and he would withdraw his hand until the man let go; he would not be seen with his knee or knees projecting beyond the knee of his companion; and whoever shook hands with him, he would turn his face toward him and would not turn away until the person had finished speaking. Narrated by al-Bazzar, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and the isnad of al-Tabarani is hasan. Majma' al-Zawa'id of al-Haythami (9/15).

[3] Ahmad in his Musnad (5/447), Ibn Majah in his Sunan (1429), and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (862) narrated from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Shibl, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade the pecking of the crow, the spreading out like a beast of prey, and that a man settle a place in the mosque as a camel settles." As for Imam Ahmad, he narrated it from the hadith of Abu Salama al-Ansari.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 27, verse 18:

The pronoun in ﴿came﴾ refers to the soldiers of Sulayman (Solomon), from among mankind, the jinn and the birds; that is, they came all together in a single row and passed by ﴿the valley of the ants﴾, meaning: the settlement of the ants(1). His saying ﴿the valley of the ants﴾ indicates that they came from the top of the mountain, or that they crossed the whole valley, as we say: so-and-so went through all the food.

Then ﴿an ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you, while they do not perceive."﴾ Why this warning? The ant took precaution in the matter, so she said ﴿while they do not perceive﴾. Thus Sulayman and his soldiers would not crush the ants' homes deliberately.

The meaning is: while they are not aware of you. This is from the justice of her judgment and her knowledge of Sulayman, and that he is neither a tyrant nor an oppressor. So the ant saw from a distance, spoke rightly, and judged justly. For all this, Sulayman smiled, laughing.

It is clear from this statement what the kingdom of the ants is distinguished by: a system in which each knows its task and performs it in the most perfect manner. This ant must have been carrying out a guarding duty, standing at a lookout, watching the air around her, as if she were an alert patrol soldier.

We have previously said: if you sat in a place and left some food scraps, for example, or sweets, you would see some ants circling around them without approaching, then they would leave. After a while you would see a group of them come and carry this piece away. It is as if the first group were the scouts who discover places of food and estimate how many ants can carry this thing.

The proof: if you doubled the piece left, you would see the number of ants that came to carry it had also doubled. And if you killed the first ant that came to scout, you would notice the ants avoided that place. Why? Because the ant that escaped death went back to her kingdom and warned them about this place.

In the kingdom of the ants there are wonders and signs. Glory be to its Creator, and glory be to Him who guided them to this engineering governed by instinct.

Among the wonders of ants: you see grains in the ants' nest split into two halves so that they do not sprout, and their nest collapses on them. But a coriander seed, for example, sprouts even when split into two halves, each half sprouting separately. Therefore, observe that the ant splits this particular seed into four parts.

Also, those interested in studying ants have noticed small white grains like the head of a pin in front of ant nests; on examination it became clear that they are seed-germ of plants carrying germinating cells, which the ants brought out so that they would not sprout.

And the Mighty God has spoken truly: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾ (al-An'am 6:38).

God Most High has called what the ant said a saying: ﴿An ant said﴾ (al-Naml 27:18). It must be that this warning ﴿enter your dwellings﴾ (al-Naml 27:18) came before Sulayman and his soldiers arrived, while they were at the edge of the valley.

The word ﴿your dwellings﴾ (al-Naml 27:18) indicates that they have houses and dwellings, a place of living and earning provision, as we say, "they gather their sustenance from here and there." Therefore you find it follows the places of food and waste, and enters them through the narrowest places. Yet we see, for example, sweet shops full of sugar, which ants love, and yet in these shops we do not find a single ant. Why? When people studied this phenomenon, they found that ants do not enter a place if there is sesame in it. This too is one of the wonders of ants.

As for His saying Most High ﴿they crush you﴾ (al-Naml 27:18): al-hatm (ḥaṭm) is breaking into pieces, and from it is His saying about the Fire: ﴿And what will make you know what is the crushing?﴾ (al-Humazah 104:5), because it crushes whatever is thrown into it.

1. Qatadah said: it was mentioned to us that it is a valley in the land of al-Sham. Ka'b said: it is at al-Ta'if. (Cited by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 7/5051.) And he said in another place: "Ka'b said: Sulayman, peace be upon him, passed by the valley of al-Sudd, one of the valleys of al-Ta'if."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 27, verse 19:

Sulayman smiled, a smile that approaches laughter. Why? Because he heard her before she reached him, and because she saw before the one seen came into view. Some have spoken on this matter and said: the wind carried the speech of the ant to him while he was still far from her. This statement might be accepted if the matter were (mechanics), but it is rather the work of a Lord and the power of a bounteous Creator who bestows favour upon whom He wills.

And he spoke, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me inspiration (awzi‘nī) ...﴾ (19), that is: prevent me from being heedless, or from forgetting these blessings, so that I may remain grateful and praising You constantly. For these blessings surpassed what He bestowed upon the general run of creation, and surpassed what He bestowed upon his brothers among the earlier prophets, and upon all the kings of the world; for he, peace be upon him, combined kingship and prophethood. Although our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was offered kingship and refused it, preferring to be a servant and messenger.

Therefore it is incumbent upon every possessor of a blessing to receive it with praise and thanks to Allah. We have previously said, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the pleasure (of life) (8)﴾ (al-Takathur), that the right of a blessing is that you praise the one who bestowed it, so you will not be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection.

Praising Allah for a blessing is like what we call in the countryside (al-Ruqubah), which is an egg that the mistress of the house places in a safe place suitable as a nest in which the hens lay eggs. When the hen sees this egg, she comes and lays upon it. Thus, thanking and praising Allah for blessings is the seed around which more of Allah's blessings gather.

This meaning has been explained in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you (7)﴾ (Ibrahim). Do you not see that whoever learns knowledge and acts upon it, Allah bequeaths to him the knowledge of what he did not know? Why? Because as long as he acts upon his knowledge, he is entrusted with knowledge; therefore Allah increases him in it and opens its locks for him. In contrast to one who learns knowledge but does not act upon it, for Allah strips him of the light of knowledge, it closes upon him, his memory rusts, and he forgets what he has learned.

And the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself (12)﴾ (Luqman), that is: the fruit of his gratitude returns to him, for if he thanks Allah with praise, Allah thanks him with increase. Therefore, among His names, exalted is He, is (al-Shakur, the Appreciative).

His saying: ﴿upon me (19)﴾ (al-Naml) is a particularity. ﴿and upon my parents (19)﴾ (al-Naml), because he inherited from them kingship and prophethood. ﴿and that I may do righteousness of which You approve (19)﴾ (al-Naml). This is the price of a blessing: that I render services of righteousness in society, so that I may be entrusted with the blessing and worthy of more of it.

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wants us to widen the circle of righteousness and the circle of goodness in society. Do you not see His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him many times over? (245)﴾ (al-Baqarah).

So He called the good you advance a loan, although He is the Giver of all blessings, and this is so that He may soften the hearts of His servants toward one another, because He is their Creator and the One who undertakes their provision.

Then He says: ﴿and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants (19)﴾ (al-Naml). He mentioned mercy and grace because they are the means of salvation; by them we enter Paradise, and without them no one will be saved. Read the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even me, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."¹

He says, glorified is He, on this meaning: ﴿Say: By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy, so in that let them rejoice (58)﴾ (Yunus). The true believer does not rejoice in his deed; rather, he rejoices if he attains the bounty and mercy of Allah, as though he is saying to his Lord: "I will not rely upon my deed, O Lord; rather, Your bounty and Your mercy are what I rely upon, for if I compared the worship You have obligated me to with the blessings and favours You have bestowed upon me, my worship would fall short of performing Your right upon me. So if You honour me with Paradise, it is by Your bounty."

Some say: how does our Lord deal with us through bounty and increase, while forbidding us dealing in usury? Is not the good deed with Him multiplied tenfold or more? We say: yes, but the increase here comes from Him, glorified and exalted is He, and is not from an equal; it is the increase of a Lord to His servants.

His saying: ﴿among Your righteous servants (19)﴾ (al-Naml) is evidence of the humility of our master Sulayman, peace be upon him. Despite his rank and station, he asks that Allah admit him among the righteous and place him in their company. He did not claim for himself any distinction, nor precedence, nor did he claim superiority over other servants of Allah, despite what Allah gave him of a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after him.

Allah gave him prophethood and entrusted him with the method, yet none of this made him arrogant or haughty, and here he asks his Lord to be among His righteous servants, just as we say: "Let me join the group, [those people]," when the car is, for example, full, and I have no seat to sit on.

Who says these words? It is Sulayman son of Dawud, peace be upon them both, whom Allah gave a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after him. Yet he preferred his servants and soldiers over himself, and he used to eat (al-Radda, coarse bran) of the flour, leaving the fine part for his subjects.

So he benefited from this kingship with nothing, and did not make for himself any of the outward displays of this kingship; rather, his Lord made it for him because he was in the aid of the servants of Allah, so Allah was in his aid. When you help your brother, you help him with your power and your limited capacities, but you are protected by the aid of Allah, the Exalted, and His power, strength and capacities which have no limits. Thus, you are the winner in this transaction.

¹ A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh). Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6463), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (2816), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Root: f-q-d (ف ق د), and all its derivatives come with the meaning of losing something. From it is the words of Allah the Exalted in the story of Joseph's brothers: ﴿They said, "We have lost the king's goblet..."﴾ — wait, the verse reads: ﴿They said, while turning towards them, "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ (Yusuf 71). If it comes in the form (tafaqqada), with doubling, it indicates that the thing exists and I am searching for it in its probable places.

So the meaning of ﴿He inspected the birds...﴾ (al-Naml 20) is that the leader or the one who oversees something must follow up on it. Sulayman (peace be upon him), when he sat in a session of knowledge or a session of judgement, looked at those present from his kingdom, as if he were the commander reviewing his soldiers. This points to the fact that he (peace be upon him), although this is his kingdom, subjected to him and obedient to his command, did not leave it neglected without follow-up.

But why did he inspect the birds in particular? They said: because he intended to undertake a journey in the desert, and the hoopoe is the expert in this matter, because it knows its water sources and sees water beneath the earth(1). They say: "as one of you sees oil in its container."

Therefore we see that among the distinctive features of the hoopoe is that Allah the Exalted made for it a long beak, because it does not eat what is on the surface of the earth, but digs with its beak to bring out its food from beneath the ground.

Do you not see that when it spoke to Sulayman about the subtleties of belief and faith in Allah, it said about the people of Sheba: ﴿...that they should not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden (al-khab' (2)) in the heavens and the earth...﴾ (al-Naml 25). So it chose this matter in particular, because it is the expert in it and its provision comes from it.

When the hoopoe was not found among those present: ﴿He said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is it among the absent?"﴾ (al-Naml 20). When a person asks about something whose reality he knows, he does not intend a question; rather, he is expressing that the hoopoe could not be absent from his session.

Therefore he said: ﴿"Why do I not see the hoopoe?"﴾ (al-Naml 20), meaning: perhaps it is present, but I do not see it for a reason on my part. Then, when he examined closely and confirmed that its place among the birds was empty, he said: ﴿"Or is it among the absent?"﴾ (al-Naml 20). Then: it must be punished: ﴿"I will surely punish it with a severe punishment, or slaughter it, or it must bring me a clear authority."﴾ (al-Naml 21)

1 Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding the verse, he said: It was mentioned to us that Sulayman wanted to cross a desert, so he summoned the hoopoe, which was the chief of the hoopoes, to learn the distance to water. He had been given a sight for this that no other bird had been given. It was mentioned to us that he could see water in the earth as one of you sees a shadow behind glass. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/349).
2 Al-Khab': the hidden thing. Al-Khab' is everything that is absent, and every absent thing that is concealed. (Lisan al-Arab, root: kh-b-'.)

Punishing the one who opposes is a necessity, because any violation that is not met with a fitting penalty will inevitably produce many other violations, greater than it. When we see an employee who is negligent in his work and no one holds him accountable, we will become like him, and disorder, laziness and indifference will spread among us. The calamity occurs when the negligent is rewarded and the undeserving is promoted.

Therefore Sulayman threatened the hoopoe: ﴿Surely I will punish him with a severe punishment, or I will slaughter him...﴾ [al-Naml 27:21].

The scholars have discussed how the hoopoe was to be punished. They said: by plucking its beautiful feathers, of which it is proud among the birds, until it becomes flesh, and then the ants are set upon it to sting it (1). Or by placing it with creatures other than its own kind, so that it finds no companion and nothing resembling it in its movement and order. Or: by assigning it to serve its peers among the hoopoes who did not disobey. Or: by gathering it with its opposites, for some birds, when gathered together, become repellent and quarrel, and some of them pluck the feathers of others, because they are opposites. Hence they said: "More constricting than prison is the company of opposites."

The poet (2) says:

"Among the miseries of this world for a man is that he sees an enemy of his, and there is no escape from being his friend."

Then the matter escalated from severe punishment to slaughter. Concerning this issue, those who rebel against the method of God, and who want to alter His rulings, have raised an objection regarding His saying about the punishment for fornication: ﴿The fornicatrix and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes...﴾ [al-Nur 24:2]. As for stoning, nothing has been reported about it. So from where did you derive it?

We say: We derived it also from the Book of God, for He, glory be to Him, said concerning the flogging of a slave-woman if she commits fornication while she is not chaste: ﴿Upon them is half of what is upon the chaste women of the punishment...﴾ [al-Nisa 4:25]. They said: "How do we halve the punishment of stoning?" This statement of theirs is evidence of their failure to understand the rulings of God.

The meaning of ﴿upon them...﴾ [al-Nisa 4:25] is: upon the slave-girls, the bondwomen, ﴿half of what is upon the chaste...﴾ [al-Nisa 4:25], the free women. He did not leave it general, but restricted the halving here to flogging, saying: ﴿of the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa 4:25]. So the slave-woman is flogged fifty lashes, and this restriction indicates that there is another punishment that is not halved, namely stoning.

Sulayman's threat to the hoopoe ends with his saying: ﴿or he must bring me a clear authority﴾ [al-Naml 27:21], that is, a clear proof justifying his absence. From the verse we understand that the subordinate may act according to his own judgment, without seeking permission from his superior, if he sees a benefit for the community that does not allow delay.

The superior, in that case, should allow his subordinate his personal judgment and seek an excuse for him, for perhaps he has a proof, and I would praise him for it and even reward him, because the time of his absence was for a public benefit, as we say colloquially: "The absent one has his excuse with him."
