In sum: if the subordinate sees a good that serves the general interest, and finds that his opportunity is narrow, he is permitted to act without permission. In the First World War, one of the German commanders acted in a way that contravened the rules of war, yet it was the cause of victory; so they gave him the Victory Medal, but they did not fail to punish him for violating the regulations and the law.

(1) Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding His saying ﴿Surely I will punish him with a severe punishment...﴾ [al-Naml 27:21]: it means plucking its feathers. ʿAbdullah ibn Shaddad said: plucking its feathers and exposing it to the sun. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/360): "Likewise said more than one of the early scholars: that he plucked its feathers and left it cast aside, to be eaten by ants and ants' kin."

(2) The poet is Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, Ahmad ibn al-Husayn, a wise poet and one of the glories of Arabic literature. He was born in Kufa (303 AH), raised in Syria, claimed prophethood in the desert of al-Samawa, then repented and retracted his claim. He was killed in 354 AH when Fatik ibn Abi Jahl al-Asadi confronted him. (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/115).

Then the Almighty says:

﴿So he [the hoopoe] tarried not long, and said: "I have comprehended that which you have not comprehended, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news."﴾ [27:22]

The meaning of ﴿tarried﴾ (fa-makatha): he stayed and settled. ﴿Not long﴾ (ghayra baeed): a short period, so he did not delay much, because he knew that he had left the assembly of Sulayman and gone without his permission; therefore he hastened his return. As soon as he reached him, he rushed to speak, ﴿and said﴾ (fa-qala), with the fa' that denotes immediacy (ta'qib), because he saw Sulayman angry and ready to punish him.

Therefore he forestalled him before he spoke and before he could rebuke him. ﴿I have comprehended that which you have not comprehended﴾: that is, I have known what you did not know. This statement is addressed to Sulayman, who ruled the whole world and to whom God subjected everything; therefore Sulayman was astonished at the hoopoe's words and eager for the news he had which Sulayman did not know.

Then the hoopoe continues: ﴿and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news﴾.

First: we pause at the beauty of expression in "Sheba" (Saba') and "news" (naba'), for between them there is a jinas naqis (imperfect paronomasia), which is one of the rhetorical embellishments (muhassinat badi'iyya) in our language. It gives the phrase a beautiful melody that harmonizes with the intended meaning. Jinas is that two words agree in letters and differ in meaning, as in the poet's words:

"I have departed from your abodes, a captive, and my heart, in your love, is a captive."

And another's saying:

"My heart has not fulfilled its duty to you by hating what is due [to be loved]..."

"A heart, whenever your remembrance passes by it, is stirred [yajibu]..."

Among perfect paronomasia (jinas tam) in the Noble Qur'an is: ﴿And on the Day the Hour comes, the criminals will swear that they tarried not but an hour﴾ [30:55].

So the Qur'anic expression ﴿and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news﴾ is beautiful in wording and precise in meaning. Do you not see that if he had said "with information" (bi-khabar) the wording and meaning would both be disturbed? For khabar refers to news in general, whereas naba' is used only for a strange, important, striking report, as in His saying: ﴿About what do they question one another? About the great news﴾ [78:1–2].

Jinas is not beautiful or effective unless it comes naturally and unaffected, such as this imperfect paronomasia in His saying: ﴿Woe to every slanderer (humazah) and backbiter (lumazah)﴾ [104:1]. The suitable word has come expressing the intended meaning without affectation: the humazah is one who finds fault in speech, and the lumazah is one who finds fault by action. The Qur'an does not hunt for a word to produce a paronomasia; rather the paronomasia comes in it naturally, as the meaning requires.

Of the same kind in the noble hadith: "Good is bound to the foreheads of horses" (al-khayl ma'qud binawasiha al-khayr), where between khayl (horses) and khayr (good) there is an imperfect paronomasia, embellishing the wording and conveying the meaning.

Sometimes a rhetorical embellishment comes forced and affected, hunted by its author, like the saying of one who carves speech, producing a crude rhymed prose: "While we were travelling, rain fell like the mouths of water-skins, and a man who was carrying grapes fell."

The meaning of ﴿I have comprehended [ahattu]...﴾: ihata means to perceive a known thing from all its sides; from it comes "the encompassing sea" (al-bahr al-muhit) for its vastness. He says, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is ever encompassing of all things﴾ [4:126]. From it also: the wall (al-ha'it) which they make around an orchard to protect and delimit it; and from it: yahtatu lil-amr (he takes precaution regarding the matter).

The circumference (muhit) of a circle surrounds its centre from every side, with an even encompassing of all its directions.

But is the hoopoe's saying to Sulayman, ﴿I have comprehended what you have not comprehended﴾, to be considered a defect in Sulayman, peace be upon him? No; rather it is considered an honour for him, because his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, subjected to him those who serve him. There is a difference between you doing a thing yourself and its being done for you; when it is done for you, this is an increase in dignity and elevation of station.

Moreover, Allah the Exalted teaches us not to conceal the talents of those beneath us, to give them the opportunity, to make room for them so that they may bring forth their abilities, and for each of them to say what he has, even if we do not know it, because it is a service to me.

Is it not a mark of honour that Sulayman has Balqis's throne brought while he is in his place? ﴿One who had knowledge of the Scripture said: "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you"﴾ [27:40].

We note that the hoopoe did not know what Sheba was, and this is evidence that Sulayman, peace be upon him, knew Sheba and its kingdom, but did not know that it was of such magnificence and such greatness.

1 Al-humazah: one who frequently engages in humz, lumz, ghamz and backbiting and defaming people (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/307). It is also said: humz and lumz have the same meaning. It is also said: humz is behind the back and in secret, and lumz is faultfinding to the face openly.
2 A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2849, 2850, 2852) from the hadith of Ibn Umar, Urwa ibn al-Ja'd and Urwa al-Bariqi, and Muslim in his Sahih (1873) from the hadith of Urwa al-Bariqi, and similarly from Urwa ibn al-Ja'd.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a mighty throne.﴾

His saying ﴿ruling over them﴾ means: a woman governs them. We have seen many women of distinction who have ruled states in the presence of men.

Then he mentions her attributes: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾. This seems to be an allusion to what Sulayman (peace be upon him) had said earlier: ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾. So she too has been given of everything relative to her peers; otherwise, Sulayman was given kingship and prophethood, which the Queen of Sheba was not given.

﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾. The throne (ʿarsh) is the seat where a ruler sits, and the throne usually corresponds to the greatness of the ruler. For example, the sheikh of the district (shaykh al-ghafar), the ʿumda, or the governor, etc., each has a chair on which he sits that suits his station. Thus, the throne is the seat of one established in authority who manages affairs.

The throne is described as mighty, although this description also applies to the Throne of Allah, the Exalted. How so? They said: it is mighty relative to the kings like her, whereas the Throne of Allah is mighty relative to all creation, with absolute greatness.

Thus the hoopoe reported to Solomon regarding the Queen of Sheba, in respect of the kingship in which she resembled Solomon as a king. Then he tells him afterwards about a matter connected with prophethood and belief in God, and this is the matter over which Solomon was jealous and became angry on its account:

﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God, and Satan has made their deeds appealing to them and has barred them from the way, so they are not guided﴾ :

That is because, when he circled the palace of Bilqis, he found in it a window through which the sun entered, as we see in the temples of the Pharaohs. In one of these temples there are openings equal to the number of the days of the year, such that the sun enters each day through one particular opening and not through the others. Likewise, Bilqis had a window like this through which the sun entered, and she would take note of it and face it.

So when he went to her with Solomon's letter, he stood at this window and blocked it with his wing, so the sun did not enter at its appointed time as the queen was accustomed to. She rose until she reached this window, and there she threw down the letter(1).

The hoopoe, then, is a believer who knows the matter of creed and belief in God, is jealous for it, and disapproves of its violation: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God...﴾ (al-Naml). He knows that God is the one truly worthy of worship, and he also knows the matter of Satan and that he is the cause of turning away from the worship of God.

﴿And Satan has made their deeds appealing to them and has barred them from the way, so they are not guided﴾ (al-Naml). So the matter is complete in his mind with all its details. Do not be surprised at the hoopoe's statement, and read: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification...﴾ (al-Isra).

It is an eloquent admonition from a firmly established preacher who understands from God, knows His method and calls to it, and it is grievous to him, and it pains his soul, that the servants turn away from God the Benefactor.

1 Al-Suyuti mentioned something similar in "al-Durr al-Manthur fi al-Tafsir bil-Ma'thur" (6/353) from Qatadah, and attributed it to Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 25:

﴿Alla (that they should not...) 25﴾ (An-Naml). It is composed of "an" (that), "la" (not), and when the two are assimilated, the nun is changed into a lam, so it becomes: alla. The meaning is: "And Satan made their deeds seem good to them, and why? So that they would not prostrate." Here there is a deleted preposition, as you say: "I wondered at (min) that so-and-so came to us," or "I wondered that so-and-so came to us."

In another reading(1), "alla" is for urging and exhortation(2).

We have said that He chose this particular attribute: ﴿Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth... 25﴾ (An-Naml), because He is expert in this matter, as He sees water in the depths of the earth just as one of you sees oil in his vessel.

What is meant by "what is hidden" in the heavens is the rain, and what is hidden in the earth is the vegetation, and from both come the necessities of life. From rainwater and the fertility of the earth comes vegetation, and on vegetation animals feed, and humans feed.

Rather, indeed the Truth, glory be to Him, ﴿knows what you conceal and what you disclose 25﴾ (An-Naml), as He said in another verse: ﴿Nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven 38﴾ (Ibrahim), and in another verse He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Say, "Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it..." 29﴾ (Ali 'Imran).

1 This is the reading of al-Zuhri, al-Kisa'i and others, meaning: "Alla, O people, prostrate!" (mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 7/5068). Al-Kisa'i said: "I never heard the elders recite it except with the light pronunciation, intending an imperative..."
2 Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: is the prostration of recitation obligatory in both readings or in one of them? I say: it is obligatory in both, because the places of prostration are either a command to prostrate, or praise of one who prostrates, or blame of one who abandons it, and one of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is a blame of the one who abandons it." (mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 7/5069).

When he spoke about the throne of Bilqis, he said: ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾ [An-Naml 27:23]. That is, relative to kings like her and to the people of her time. But when [the phrase] ﴿the mighty throne﴾ [An-Naml 27:26] is known, it refers only to the throne of Allah, exalted is He, for He alone has absolute greatness before all creation.

﴿He said, "We shall see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars."﴾

﴿He said, "We shall see..."﴾ [An-Naml 27:27]. Seeing has its place in the eye, but can truthfulness or falsehood be known by the eye? No. The word has shifted from seeing with the eye to knowing through proof, so it means "we shall know." We also say, "This matter needs looking into" (fihi nazar), meaning it requires study and careful examination.

In this verse there is a manifestation of the courtesy of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and his gentleness toward his subjects. He is the lord whose command is obeyed, yet he says to the hoopoe: ﴿Have you told the truth or were you among the liars?﴾ [An-Naml 27:27]. Truthfulness is opposed by lying, but the courtesy of prophethood forbids him to accuse one of his soldiers of lying outright, so he says: ﴿or were you among the liars?﴾

That is, even if you did lie, you are not unique in it, for many people lie. Or the phrase "among the liars" may mean that he leans toward giving him the benefit of the doubt and keeps him close. This shows that, through his inspiration (ilham) as a prophet, he knew the hoopoe was truthful, but since the matter was open to examination, he had to verify it, and he would not flatter one of his own soldiers.

1 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5071): "In the words ﴿Have you told the truth or were you among the liars?﴾ [An-Naml 27:27] is evidence that the ruler must accept the excuse of his subjects and ward off punishment from them based on the apparent circumstances of their excuses, because Sulayman did not punish the hoopoe when it offered its excuse to him. Rather, the hoopoe's truthfulness became an excuse, because it reported something that required striving (jihad)."

"He said: 'We shall see (sananzuru)...'" (Qur'an 27:27). Seeing is properly the function of the eye, but can truth and falsehood be known by the eye? No. So the word has passed from seeing with the eye to knowing through proof, and it means "we shall know." We say, "This matter needs looking into (nazar)," meaning it requires study and careful scrutiny.

In the verse there is a manifestation of the courtesy (adab) of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his gentleness toward his subjects. He is the lord who is obeyed, yet he says to the hoopoe: "Have you spoken the truth, or have you been among the liars?" (Qur'an 27:27). Truthfulness (sidq) is opposed by lying (kadhib), but Sulayman (peace be upon him), by the courtesy of prophethood, refuses to accuse one of his soldiers of lying outright, so he says: "Or have you been among the liars?"

That is, even if lying has come from you, you are not unique in it, for many of creation lie. Or: "among the liars" means inclining toward them and being close to them. This indicates that, by his inspirations as a prophet, he knows that he is truthful. However, since the matter is still under examination, we must verify it, and I will not flatter a soldier of mine.

This is the view Solomon settled on in order to test the hoopoe's truthfulness: that he should send it with a letter from him to these people. Here is one of the manifestations of the eloquent concision (al-ijaz al-baligh) of the noble Qur'an. After Solomon said ﴿We shall see...﴾ [27:27], he said ﴿Take this letter of mine...﴾ [27:28].

Was the letter already prepared and ready? No. Rather, the implied sense is: he said, "We shall see whether you have spoken the truth or were among the liars." Then he wrote to her a letter containing such-and-such, and then he said to the hoopoe: ﴿Take this letter of mine...﴾ [27:28]. This has been omitted because it is known from the context of the story.

As for His saying ﴿...then withdraw from them...﴾ [27:28], it means: move away a little, and try to find out ﴿what they will return [in discussion]﴾ [27:28], meaning: some of them will consult one another and discuss what is in the letter. Of this kind is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them a word, and that it does not possess for them any harm or benefit?﴾ [20:89].

The context requires us to say: So the hoopoe went off with the letter, dropped it before Bilqis, and she read it and consulted her followers and her close advisers concerning it. Then she said: ﴿O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾ [27:29].

We notice here the speed of the response to the command ﴿Go... 28﴾ (An-Naml). Immediately after it, the Queen of Sheba said: ﴿O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me. 29﴾ (An-Naml). This indicates that Solomon's commands were surrounded by swift execution; therefore the context omitted all the details between the command ﴿Go... 28﴾ (An-Naml) and the response ﴿She said... 29﴾ (An-Naml), coming directly in this manner of haste.

The meaning of ﴿al-Mala'(chiefs)... 29﴾ (An-Naml) is: the notables and nobles of the people, their counselors and their inner circle. ﴿Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me. 29﴾ (An-Naml). She described the letter as "noble"(1), either because she had heard of Solomon, peace be upon him, and the greatness of his kingdom, or because the letter was written on fine paper in a beautiful hand, and furthermore it was sealed with his official seal, which indicates that it is an important letter that deserves study and consultation about it(2).

1. Several sayings and reports have been transmitted regarding the meaning of "noble" here, among them:
- Its contents are good: said by Qatadah, as related from him by Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.
- Sealed: said by Ibn Abbas, as related from him by Ibn Mardawayh. (Both are cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 6/353.)
2. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5074): "She described it as noble because of what it contained of gentle speech and admonition in calling to the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and good appeal and winning of hearts, without containing abuse or cursing, nor anything that would disturb the soul, and without harsh or obscure speech, in keeping with the manner of the messengers in calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

**Idhan** (then, so): She knows Solomon, his prophethood and his qualities, and that he writes to them in the name of Allah and issues his call to them on the commands of Allah. The content of the letter, after "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," was: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, but come to me in submission﴾ ﴿31﴾

This is a brief telegram, in the most eloquent conciseness. ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, but come to me in submission.﴾ [27:31]. Here "exalt" (ʿulūw) means the arrogance and self-importance that kings in particular are wont to adopt, and she is one of them: a queen who has a mighty throne, and has been given of everything. That he addresses her in this concise tone, far from debate and dispute, is a matter that requires from her consideration and deliberation.

Therefore, after she had informed her counselors about the matter of the letter and what it contained, she asked them for their opinion and counsel:

﴿She said, "O chiefs, give me your opinion in my affair. I would not decide a matter until you are present with me."﴾ [27:32]

We have previously discussed the meaning of fatwa (legal opinion), and that it derives from futuwwah, meaning strength. It is like the saying "ghaniya fulan" (so-and-so became rich), meaning he became wealthy by himself, and "aghnahu ghayruh" (another made him wealthy), meaning he supplied him with wealth. Likewise, "aftahu" means he gave him strength in judgment and argument.

He said: ﴿in my affair﴾ [27:32], even though the matter concerns the whole state and not her alone, because she is the symbol of the state and of the kingship, and if Solomon confronts her, he will first damage her rule and harm her prestige before that of her subjects.

﴿I would not decide a matter until you are present with me﴾ [27:32] means: I do not settle any matter except in your presence and after consulting you. This indicates that she followed the principle of consultation (shura), despite her kingship, dominion and authority.

The Mala' of her people replied to her:

﴿They said, "We are people of strength and of mighty might (1), and the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ 

That is: we are people of strength in our bodies, and people of courage and might, meaning armies with numbers and equipment. ﴿And the command is yours…﴾ That is: if you see war, we are ready and prepared. They present their opinion to her without binding her to it; it is a political opinion, not a military directive, and she is the one who decides on war if she wishes. ﴿…so consider what you will command.﴾ That is: we are prepared for peace and for war, and we await your command.

(1) Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that the people of her counsel were three hundred and twelve men, each man having ten thousand men under him. Related by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim. Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/357), and by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5077).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 34:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿She said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the honored among its people humiliated. And thus do they do."﴾

Balqis presents her opinion: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it...﴾ (An-Naml). That is because they desire dominion, so they plunder everything they pass by, and they even destroy and corrupt. Why? Because at the moment the conquering king arrives, he cannot guarantee victory; therefore he destroys everything. Then, once he knows that he has prevailed and that affairs have settled for him, he preserves things and does not destroy them.

﴿...and make the honored among its people humiliated...﴾ (An-Naml). This is because the kingship is built upon the ruins of an older kingdom, so the people of honor and sovereignty are the first to be targeted, since the matter has been taken out of their hands, and they will strive to recover it. There must be among them resentment and fierce hostility in disputes.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And thus do they do﴾ (An-Naml), the scholars have differing views about it. They said(1) that it is from the words of Balqis, as a conclusion (tadhyil) to her previous statement. But what does ﴿And thus do they do﴾ (An-Naml) add after she said ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the honored among its people humiliated...﴾ (An-Naml)?

The correct opinion is that this phrase is from the Truth(2), glory be to Him and exalted, to confirm her words, and that she was correct in her opinion: kings do thus when they enter a town. This indicates that the Truth, glory be to Him, is the Lord of all creation, and when He hears from one of His servants a word of truth, He supports him in it, does not show partisanship against him, and does not deprive him of his right.

(1) Said by Ibn Shajarah, as transmitted from him by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5087), and he said: "It was said: it is from the speech of Balqis, as an emphasis on the meaning she intended."

(2) Said by Ibn 'Abbas, who said: it is from the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, informing Muhammad (ﷺ) and his ummah of that and making it known. Transmitted by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5078), and something similar was mentioned by al-Suyuti in "al-Durr al-Manthur" (6/357), attributing it to Ibn Abi Hatim.

After her counselors had left the matter and its management to her, she began to exercise her mind, employing her shrewdness and her experience of the lives of kings. She said: "If Sulayman is a king, he will covet our wealth; but if he is a prophet, he will not concern himself with any of it." So she resolved to send him a gift befitting his station as a king and her own station as well, to prove to him that she is possessed of great wealth and abundance.

A gift must have been valuable enough to win over the king—or, as we say, "to sway him or bend him" (tulawwihuhu aw tulawwihu).

﴿And I am sending them a gift, and I will wait to see with what the messengers return.﴾ (An-Naml 35). If he is a king, he will accept it; and we know that his practice is to take some of the tribute and the wealth that is driven to him every year. But if he is a prophet, he will accept nothing from her. This is a fine opinion from Bilqis, indicating her shrewdness, intelligence and sound judgment, for she spared her people the calamities of war and confrontation.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 36:

Meaning: When the messenger of Bilqis came to Sulayman with the gift, [Sulayman] said: ﴿Do you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you...﴾ So what kind of gift is this, when I possess a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after me? ﴿Rather...﴾ meaning: turn away from the previous speech, ﴿you rejoice in your gift.﴾

He attributed the gift to them, not to himself. The idafa (annexation construction) may carry the sense of the preposition lam (for), as in "qalam Zayd" meaning "Zayd's pen"; or the sense of min (from), as in "irdabb qamh" meaning "an irdabb of wheat"; or the sense of fi (in), as in "makr al-layl" meaning "the scheming of the night."

So his words ﴿with your gift﴾ may mean: a gift for you, that is, you rejoice if a gift comes to you from someone; or because I will return it to you, so you rejoice in its return, like someone who says "a blessing, O one who gathers" (a saying of congratulation); or a gift from you, that is, you rejoice if you give me a gift and I accept it from you.

These are three meanings of his words ﴿Rather, you rejoice in your gift.﴾

1 That is: what He has given me of Islam, kingship and prophethood is better than what He has given you, so I do not rejoice in wealth. (Said by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 7/5084.)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 37:

We mention that the queen said: ﴿So I am going to send them a gift, and will see with what the envoys return.﴾ (An-Naml 27:35) It is as if he (Solomon) senses the content of what she said, and speaks out of the illuminations of prophethood within it, saying: ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with hosts they cannot withstand, and we will surely expel them from there, humiliated, and they will be debased.﴾ (An-Naml 27:37)

Thus the matter entered the stage of confrontation, because our speech is the speech of prophethood, which does not accept compromise, not the speech of a king who strives for the trinkets of this world.

﴿And we will surely expel them from there, humiliated, and they will be debased.﴾ (An-Naml 27:37) It is as if he is revealing to them the words of their queen: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the most honorable of its people its lowest.﴾ (An-Naml 27:34) And this too is one of the illuminations of prophethood.

The meaning of ﴿we have no power against them﴾ (An-Naml 27:37): one says, "I have no power against such-and-such," meaning: I cannot confront it, and I am too weak to confront it, or I have no capacity for it. ﴿And we will surely expel them from there, humiliated﴾ (An-Naml 27:37) because he will strip them of their kingship, so that after they were kings they become slaves. Then he intensifies his harshness toward them with ﴿and they will be debased﴾ (An-Naml 27:37), because they might accept the state of servitude and the life of subjects, so he added ﴿and they will be debased﴾ (An-Naml 27:37), since debasement (ṣighār) occurs only through killing and captivity.

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says:

﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾

Al-Mala' (the chiefs): the nobles of a people, their leaders, and the people of opinion among them. ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ (An-Naml). Here too is a manifestation of the illuminations of prophethood in Sulayman: he knows what will happen among them when their gift is returned to them, and that they will hasten to Islam. So returning the gift means that we are people of a word, a message and a principle we defend, not people of worldly interest.

And when he knew that they would come to him in submission, he asked his soldiers to bring him her throne, and he set the time for bringing this throne: ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾ (An-Naml).

So (then): it is necessary to go to the kingdom of Sheba, dismantle the throne, carry it to the kingdom of Solomon, and then reassemble it there. This is naturally a task beyond human capacity, so none of them spoke up; even the ordinary jinn did not offer Solomon their readiness for this task.

﴿A ifrit (1) of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place (2), and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾

The jinn are like humans in power and skill: among them are the strong and skilful, and among them are the weak who are good at nothing. It is said (a dialect expression) that ʿifrit (ʿifrīt) comes from ʿafr (dust-throwing) (ʿafr), for when they used to race one another on foot or on horses and others, whoever was ahead would throw dust in the face of the one behind, hindering him from overtaking. So they said: ʿifrīt, meaning one who covers (ʿaffara) the one behind him. Or the meaning is that he rubs the face of whoever opposes him with dust, and so he was named ʿifrīt.

So the ʿifrīt is the cunning, wicked one among the jinn, and the one possessing extraordinary strength among them. He is the one who offered himself for this task, and he said: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place...﴾ (An-Naml).

This is a general statement, because Solomon's sitting among his subjects for judgment or for consultation would take time: an hour or two, for example. The ʿifrīt pledged to bring the throne within this time, meaning he would not delay it until another sitting.

His saying ﴿and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it﴾ (An-Naml) indicates that this ifrit knows the magnificence and immensity of this throne, and that it is a precious thing deserving care, especially in the process of transporting it. Therefore he said, regarding its size and bulk, "I am strong for it," able to carry it, and regarding its preciousness and splendour, "I am trustworthy for it," I will not squander anything of it.

(1) ʿIfrīt: one who is forceful in matters, with exaggeration, together with cunning and guile. (Lisan al-ʿArab, root ʿ-f-r.)

(2) Al-Suddi and others said: Solomon used to sit for judgment, governance and meals from the beginning of the day until the sun declined. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/363.)

Then another man spoke, whom the Qur'an did not identify except by description (3):

﴿He said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." And when he saw it placed beside him, he said, "This is from the favor of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself; and whoever is ungrateful — indeed, my Lord is Free of need and Generous."﴾ (40)

Al-taraf: the upper eyelid of the eye.

The scholars have spoken about this verse. First: they said that "[the Book]..." (27:40) refers to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), from which God gives some of His creatures knowledge of secrets. As for "the one who had knowledge of the Book," they said he was Asif ibn Barkhiya, a righteous man whom God had made aware of the secrets of the universe.

Others said: rather, it was Solomon (peace be upon him). When the ifrit said to him, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place..." (27:39), [the man] said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you..." (27:40), because if he were another person, he would have had a superiority over Solomon in knowledge of the Book.

However, they replied to them that it is part of Solomon's greatness that one of his subjects should possess this knowledge; the one who has knowledge of the Book, to the extent that he brings the throne before the blink of an eye, is a servant in Solomon's kingdom and subjected to him. Just as possessing attributes does not necessarily imply superiority, and it is not a condition of kingship that the king know everything; otherwise we would say to the king: "Come and fix the toilets for us."

As for us, we incline to the view that it was Solomon (peace be upon him).

There is a great difference in capability between one who brings the throne before the king rises from his assembly, and one who brings it in the blink of an eye. Moving the throne from the kingdom of Bilqis to the kingdom of Solomon requires time and strength.

Time is inversely proportional to strength: the more strength increases, the less time is needed. For example, when a small child is asked to move something from one place to another, he goes slowly, carries it slowly, until he places it in its spot; but a man, with his hand, moves it quickly. We notice this matter in means of transport: there is a difference between travelling by car, travelling by airplane, and travelling by rocket, for example.

We have discussed this in the story of the "Night Journey and Ascension" (al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken by night with this speed, because God Most High carried him by night and transported him from one place to another; therefore the journey came with a speed beyond human imagination.

And since time is proportional to strength, the event is not attributed to the Messenger of God, but to God, to the Power of powers, which does not need time at all. If you say: "Why, then, did the journey take a night and require time?" We say: because he (ﷺ) passed by things, saw things, spoke, asked, and heard; it is this that occupied the time, whereas the Night Journey itself has no time.

Therefore, before telling us of this wondrous event, He—blessed and exalted—said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night...﴾ (17:1), meaning: He is exalted above resembling others. Likewise, the matter of transporting the throne in the blink of an eye: whoever did it must have done it with help from God and with knowledge that God gave him; he moved it by "Be" (kun), which requires neither time nor strength. And since it is by God's will, power and inspiration, we say nothing but: Amen.

In His saying to the jinn, ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you...﴾ (27:40), there is a challenge to the ifrit of the jinn, so that he does not think he is stronger than the human being: "If God wills to grant me a strength by which I surpass you, and subject you to serve me."

Among this is His saying, glory be to Him, concerning the subjugation of the jinn: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries, statues, basins like reservoirs, and stationary cooking pots...﴾ (34:13).

And so that they would know that they were ignorant: they kept working for Solomon while he was dead, leaning on his staff before them, while they were terrified and afraid of him.

The challenge may be by elevation, and it may be by nearness, like the one who said to his companion: "I have studied Paris in detail, and I can ride with you in the car and tell you where we are and in front of which place, while I have my eyes closed." The other said: "I can tell you that without closing my eyes."

As for His saying ﴿And when he saw it placed beside him...﴾ (27:40), that is, the throne, ﴿he said, "This is from the favor of my Lord..."﴾ (27:40): either because He enabled him to bring it himself, or because He subjected to him one who had knowledge of the Book, who brought it to him; either this or that is a favor from God.

﴿To test me...﴾ (27:40): to examine me. ﴿Whether I will be grateful or ungrateful...﴾ (27:40): that is, will I thank God and thus succeed in this test, or will I be ungrateful for God's blessing and thus fail in it? For a test is only judged by its outcome.

Gratitude is to attribute the blessing to its Giver, and not to let the beauty of the blessing distract one from the majesty of the One who bestowed and granted it, so that one would say, for example: "I was given it only because of knowledge I possess."

As for His saying ﴿And whoever is grateful is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself...﴾ (27:40): that is, God Most High does not increase in anything by our thanks; He, glory be to Him and exalted, has the attributes of absolute perfection before anyone thanks Him. Whoever gives thanks, it returns to him, and it is the fruit of his gratitude.

﴿And whoever is ungrateful...﴾ (27:40): that is, denies the blessing and does not thank the Bestower. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Free of need...﴾ (27:40): that is, from his thanks. ﴿...and Generous﴾ (27:40): that is, He gives to His servant despite what he has done of denial and ingratitude for the blessing, because His blessings are numerous and cannot be counted; and this is from His forbearance and mercy toward His creatures.

Therefore, when we reflect on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it...﴾ (14:34), this expression appears verbatim in two verses of the Book of God, which led some to see in it a repetition without benefit. But if we look at the ending of each of them, we find them different:

The first concludes with His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is ever a wrongdoer, ungrateful﴾ (14:34), while the other: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (16:18).

So they are complementary; each has its own meaning. The first shows the wrongdoing of man when he denies and rejects the blessing of God upon him, and the other adds that God, despite that, is Forgiving to His servant and Merciful to him.

And we note in the verse ﴿And if you should count...﴾ (14:34) the use of "in" (in), which indicates doubt, because no one dares to count the blessings of God in the universe; they are beyond limit. Therefore no one has undertaken this matter, although with their modern means they have counted everything except the blessings of God; no one in any institute or university specializing in statistics has undertaken to count them.

This is evidence that they are definitively beyond human capacity, just as we have not found, for example, anyone who undertook to count the grains of sand in the desert. And we pause at His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿The favor of God﴾ (14:34), and He did not say "blessings of God" (ni'am); the inability to count is before a single blessing, because beneath it are many blessings, which if you traced them you would find beyond count.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 41:

Then, when Bilqis came to him, he wanted to test her intelligence and her faith:

﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; let us see whether she will be guided or whether she will be among those who are not guided."﴾ 

His words ﴿Disguise...﴾ (al-Naml) are the opposite of "recognize," because he brought the throne in its own form as it was with her in Saba'. Had she seen it in its original state, she would have said, "It is it," and his (Sulayman's) test of her intelligence would not have appeared. Therefore he said ﴿Disguise her throne for her...﴾ (al-Naml), meaning: change some of its features, and from this comes the word "mutanakkir" (a person in disguise), who alters his features and clothing so that those around him do not recognize him.

﴿Let us see whether she will be guided or whether she will be among those who are not guided﴾ (al-Naml): "guided" in faith to Islam, or "guided" by reason to the answer concerning the throne.

Footnote 1: Ibn 'Abbas said: he removed its gems and handles. Mujahid said: he ordered it to be changed; what was red was made yellow, what was yellow was made red, and what was green was made red, altering everything from its state. 'Ikrimah said: they added to it and subtracted from it. Qatadah said: he made its bottom its top and its front its back, and they added to it and subtracted from it. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/364).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 42:

The question came in this form: ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾ (al-Naml 27:42), in order to obscure the matter of the throne for her and to test the precision of her observation. Had he said to her, "Is this your throne?", that would have been a hint to her of the answer. Rather, ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾ is as if he were saying: "This is not your throne." Then, when she looked at it in general terms, she recognized that it was her throne. But when she saw the alteration and the changes in it, she thought it was other than it. Therefore she chose a diplomatic answer that could encompass this and that, and she said: ﴿It is as if it were it.﴾ (al-Naml 27:42) At that, Sulayman understood that she possessed a great degree of intelligence, shrewdness and soundness of judgment.

Likewise, the speech of politicians and diplomats is speech that suits all possibilities and any reality that follows it. If the matter turns out contrary to what they said, they precede it with words: "Did I not tell you such-and-such?"

Among such examples is what Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan said to al-Ahnaf ibn Qays(1): "O Ahnaf, why do you not revile Ali from the pulpit as people revile him?" Al-Ahnaf said: "Excuse me, O Commander of the Faithful." Mu'awiya said: "I have resolved upon you unless you do it." He said: "Since you have resolved upon me, I will ascend the pulpit, but I will say to the people: 'The Commander of the Faithful Mu'awiya has ordered me to curse Ali, so say with me: May the curse of God be upon him.'" Thereupon Mu'awiya said: "No, O Ahnaf, do not say anything."

Why? Because the curse in this situation would return to whom? To Mu'awiya or to Ali?

And there is told the story of the one-eyed tailor who sewed a robe for one of the poets, and when it came, one of its sleeves was longer than the other, so he could not wear it. When they asked him why he did not wear the new robe, he informed them of what the tailor had done. They said: "Satirize him." So he said:

"I composed a poem that does not know
whether it is praise or satire:
Amr sewed me a qaba',
would that his two eyes were equal."

The statement admits of two meanings: a supplication for him (praise), and a supplication against him (satire). This is the diplomatic reply by which its speaker escapes confrontation.

Likewise Bilqis gave a diplomatic answer: ﴿It is as if it were it.﴾ (al-Naml 27:42) As for ﴿And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims﴾ (al-Naml 27:42), it may be a continuation of Bilqis' speech, meaning: we were given knowledge before this incident, and we knew that you are a prophet when you returned the gift to us and said what you said, so we had no need of such an incident to know your prophethood.

It may also be from the speech of Sulayman, peace be upon him.

1 He is Abu Bahr, chief of the Banu Tamim, one of the great, shrewd and eloquent men, proverbial for forbearance. He was born in Basra (3 BH), and met the Prophet (ﷺ) but did not see him. He took part in the conquests in Khurasan, withdrew from the strife on the day of the Camel, then fought at Siffin with Ali. He died in Kufa in the year 72 AH at the age of 69. (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli, 1/276).

Meaning: What Solomon did of events and what he showed her of signs turned her away from the disbelief to which she had been accustomed. ﴿Indeed, she had been among a disbelieving people﴾ (An-Naml 27:43). So Solomon, by what he did, turned her away from what she used to worship besides Allah.

**al-Ṣarḥ** (the palace or hall): it is either the lofty, elaborate palace, or the great hall where kings sit, such as the Iwan of Kisra (Khosrow) for example. When she entered, ﴿he thought it was a pool﴾ (al-Naml 27:44), she supposed it was water. When a person sees water or wetness in front of him, he mechanically and involuntarily lifts his garments so that they do not get wet. Therefore Balqis uncovered her shins, meaning she lifted the hem of her robe.

Here Sulayman alerted her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass﴾ (27:44), meaning: enter, do not fear any wetness, for this is not a body of water, but a palace paved smooth with glass, meaning built of glass and crystal, so that the water moves beneath it, with the fish in it.

﴿She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾ (27:44), first by disbelief, and by evil assumption about Sulayman, that he wanted to drown her in a pool of water. ﴿And I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (27:44). It appears that she did not utter the word of Islam explicitly until this moment, and that the earlier statement ﴿and we were Muslims﴾ (27:42) was spoken by Sulayman, peace be upon him.

Her saying ﴿and I have submitted with Sulayman﴾ (27:44) is like the saying of the magicians to Pharaoh when they saw the miracle: ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ (20:70), because faith is directed to Allah, and the Messenger is the one who points to Allah. Therefore she said ﴿and I have submitted with Sulayman﴾ (27:44) and did not say "I have submitted to Sulayman." Indeed, she had come under his authority and was convinced of his prophethood, but the pride of kingship within her prevented her from submitting to him and from announcing her Islam to Allah along with Sulayman, since he was the cause of that. It is as if she were saying to him: "Do not think that I have submitted to you; rather I have submitted with you." Thus, you and I are equal; neither of us exalts himself over the other, for both of us are servants of Allah.

Some Israeliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) have entered this story, among them that Sulayman, peace be upon him, made the palace in this form so that Balqis would uncover her shins, because he had heard that her shins were hairy, along with other fabrications that do not befit the station of prophethood.¹

¹ Ibn Kathir mentioned this story in his tafsir (3/365) and attributed it to Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Suddi and Ibn Jarir. Dr. Muhammad Abu Shahba also mentioned it in his book "al-Isra'iliyyat wa'l-Mawdu'at fi Kutub al-Tafsir" (p. 348).

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, brings us to another Prophet in the procession of the Prophets:

﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah," but they became two factions contending.﴾

The story of the Prophet of Allah Salih (peace be upon him) with his people Thamud has passed us by in Surat ash-Shu'ara', and it is mentioned again here, because the Qur'an recounts to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the procession of the Prophets that which strengthens his heart. Whenever he encounters events that shake the heart, Allah gives him a portion of the Qur'an suited to the circumstances he is passing through. This is not a repetition of the events; rather it is a distribution of scenes, such that when they are gathered together, they complete the construction of the story.

As for His, glory be to Him, saying ﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih...﴾ (an-Naml), he must have been sent with something. What is it? ﴿that worship Allah...﴾ (an-Naml). Therefore the "an" is called the explanatory "an" (an tafsiriyyah), as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses...﴾ (al-Qasas) What? ﴿that suckle him...﴾ (al-Qasas).

The explanation may also come as a clause, as in: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him...﴾ (Ta-Ha, 120). By what? ﴿He said, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ (Ta-Ha, 120).

So the explanation of the whispering, which is a general matter, is given by His saying ﴿O Adam...﴾ (Ta-Ha, 120). Thus our message to Thamud is summarized and its substance is ﴿that worship Allah...﴾ (an-Naml).

Worship, as we have mentioned, is to obey Allah by doing what He has commanded and by abstaining from what He has forbidden and warned against. As for what has neither command nor prohibition concerning it, it is among the permissible matters: if you wish, you do it, and if you wish, you leave it. When we survey the movements of living beings and the vicegerents on earth, we find that 5% of their movements fall under the scope of "do" and "do not", and the rest is permissible.

Thus: obligation is attached to things you must do, because in them is the righteousness of your society, or things you must abstain from, because in them is the corruption of your society.

So what was the outcome?

﴿Then they were two factions contending.﴾ (an-Naml)

"Contending" (ikhtisam) means that one faction stands against the other. The meaning is that one faction of them worshipped Allah and obeyed, while the other faction opposed and disbelieved in Allah.

Some who love to attack Islam and the style of the Qur'an have stopped at this verse. They lack the Arabic linguistic faculty that helps them understand the speech of Allah, and even if they have learned it, their souls are not pure enough to receive the speech of Allah, and there is in them malice and bad intention.

Their objection is that ﴿two factions...﴾ (an-Naml) is dual, while ﴿contending﴾ (an-Naml) indicates the plural, so why did it not say "yakhtasimani" (the two contend)? This is the usage of the Qur'an in several places, including His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And if two groups among the believers fight, then make peace between them. And if one of them oppresses the other, then fight against the one that oppresses until it returns to the ordinance of Allah. And if it returns, then make peace between them...﴾ (al-Hujurat, 9). By analogy it should say "faqtatalata" (the two fought). But when we reflect on the meaning, we find that a ta'ifah (group) is a body of people facing another body; if fighting occurs, each of them takes up arms, rather than one group advancing with a single sword. So in the state of fighting they are a plurality.

Therefore He said "iqtatalu" (they fought) in the plural form. At the beginning, however, when the fighting is determined, each group has one opinion expressed by its leader; thus in this state they are dual.

Likewise, although the word ta'ifah is singular in form, it is applied only to a group, so each individual of the group stands with his sword facing another from the other group.

And here too, ﴿two factions...﴾ (an-Naml), that is, believers and disbelievers, ﴿contending﴾ (an-Naml), because each individual in this body stands facing an individual of the other body.

In another place, the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, explained this matter, saying, glory be to Him:

﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them; boiling water will be poured over their heads, by which what is in their bellies and skins will be melted. And for them are maqami' (rods) of iron. Whenever they wish to get out of it, from distress, they will be returned to it, and [it will be said], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ (al-Hajj, 19–22)

As for the other faction: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk. And they were guided to good speech and were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.﴾ (al-Hajj, 23–24)

Thus the Truth, glory be to Him, made clear each of the two factions, and clarified their end and their recompense.

Here we notice the word ﴿fa-idha﴾ (an-Naml), which the grammarians call the "fuja'iyyah" (sudden "then"), and they illustrate it by their saying: "I went out, and suddenly there was a lion at the door." The meaning is that you were surprised by something you did not expect. Likewise it happened with the disbelievers of the people of Thamud when their Prophet said to them ﴿that worship Allah...﴾ (an-Naml). Yet they surprise us: they are two factions, believers and disbelievers.

The logic of reason, truth and sound nature requires that they receive this matter with obedience and submission, and not differ in it to this degree: one faction in Paradise and another in the Blaze. ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.﴾ (al-Infitar, 13–14)

They said: Indeed Allah, exalted is He, does not send Messengers except upon corruption in society. The Creator, mighty and majestic, created in man the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah) that turns him back to his right mind and forbids him; and the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah) that has been reassured by faith and has entrusted Allah with judgment regarding "do" and "do not"; and the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su'), which is the one that does not recognize what is good, nor denounce what is evil, and calls its owner only to wrongdoing.

And Allah, mighty and majestic, is the Lord (Rabb), and it is the habit of a lord to look after the one he nurtures so that he attains his goal in the most perfect manner. Have you seen a father who raises his children except for a purpose? Since He, glory be to Him, is my Lord, He does not command me except for my good and the good of my society. None of our obedience benefits Him, and none of our disobedience harms Him, because He, glory be to Him, created the whole universe with absolute perfect attributes. Thus sound nature requires receiving the commands of Allah with acceptance and submission.

This contention gathers the believers in one direction, because they agreed upon faith, and the disbelievers in another direction, because they agreed upon disbelief. But the believers are distinguished in that their accord continues to the end of their lives, and even at the meeting with Allah, exalted is He, in Paradise, because they agreed in the world on the plan of action and in the Hereafter on the ultimate reward, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous.﴾ (az-Zukhruf, 67)

As for the disbelievers, disputes will arise among them on the Day of Resurrection, and they will curse one another and disown one another. When the Qur'an depicts the contention of the people of the Fire, after mentioning the bliss of the people of Paradise, it says:

﴿That is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return: Hell, which they will burn in, so wretched is the resting place. This—so let them taste it: a boiling liquid and a dark, pus-like fluid, and other [punishments] of similar kinds in pairs. This is a company rushing in with you. No welcome for them; indeed, they will burn in the Fire. They will say, "Rather, [it is] you; no welcome for you. You brought this upon us, so wretched is the settlement." They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us—increase for him double punishment in the Fire." And they will say, "Why do we not see men whom we used to count among the bad? Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?" Indeed, that is the truth: the contention of the people of the Fire.﴾ (Sad, 55–64)

Thus, the contention in the world is between a believer and a disbeliever, while in the Hereafter it is among the disbelievers themselves: between those who misled and those who were misled, between those who followed and those who were followed.

[Footnote 1] al-maqami': plural of miqma'ah, a piece of wood or iron with which an animal is struck to humiliate it and make it obey. His saying ﴿And for them are maqami' of iron﴾ (al-Hajj) means they will be struck with them; whenever they wish to leave the Fire, they will be returned to it by being beaten with the maqami' in humiliation for them. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/134)

[Footnote 2] al-hamim is among the words with opposite meanings: it can mean cold water and it can mean hot water. Al-hamim also means sweat. (Lisan al-Arab, root h-m-m). Al-ghassaq is what drips and flows from the skins of the people of the Fire and their pus, such as pus and the like. (Lisan al-Arab, root gh-s-q)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 46:

Since the story of Thamud was mentioned in al-Shu'ara', nothing was said there about hastening evil. What is the evil they hastened, which their Lord, glorified and exalted is He, rebukes them for? It is their saying: ﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾ (al-A'raf 70).

How strange is the matter of these people! What would they do if the evil befell them? They all said together: "When the evil comes to us, we will seek forgiveness and repent." They think that seeking forgiveness and repentance will be accepted from them at that time.

But the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment﴾ (al-Nisa' 17-18).

So why do you hasten evil and punishment, when it was incumbent upon you to hasten good? Your hastening of evil stands between you and good, because it will not be accepted from you: ﴿Why do you not seek forgiveness of Allah, that you may receive mercy?﴾ (al-Naml 46).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 47:

Al-tayr (the omen-bird): He used the birds. This was a practice they resorted to when attending to their affairs or when traveling, for example. One of them would hold a bird and then release it. If it flew toward the right, he took it as a good omen (tafa'ul) and went ahead with the task; if it flew toward the left, he took it as a bad omen (tasha'um) and refrained from what he was about to do. They called these the sanihat and the barihat(1). So the meaning is: "We take you and those who follow you as a bad omen."

﴿Qala ta'irukum 'inda Allah...﴾ (47) (al-Naml). That is: it is a decree decreed upon you. The bird has no part in your destinies or in what befalls you of rulings. So how do you take from its movement a starting point for your own movement? Rather, your omen and what is decreed for you is from Allah, a decree that He decrees.

In the verse of Ya Sin: ﴿Qalu ta'irukum ma'akum...﴾ (19) (Ya Sin), that is: your bad omen is your disbelief to which you clung.

But why did the bad omen come up here, when their prophet was calling them to Allah? They said: because as soon as he came to them they opposed him, so a severe drought struck them and the sky withheld its rain from them, and they said: "It is he who has brought upon us the drought and ruin."

As for His saying: ﴿Bal antum qawmun tuftanun﴾ (47) (al-Naml), al-fitnah (trial) means either testing and affliction, or the fitnah of gold in the fire.

1. al-Sani\h: whatever comes to you from your right, such as a gazelle, a bird or something else; al-Barih: whatever comes to you of that from your left (Lisan al-Arab, root: s-n-h).

This matter is also a new snapshot of the story that was not mentioned in al-Shu'ara'. Thus is all of the Qur'anic narrative: if a person reflects on it, he will find it to be scattered snapshots, each of which adds something new and addresses a matter suited to the Qur'anic portion (najm) in which it was revealed, to strengthen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-rahṭ (a collective noun with no singular from its own root) denotes a number from three to ten. So the meaning of ﴿tis'atu rahṭin﴾ (Surah an-Naml, 48) is as if they were tribes, clans or factions: the tribe of so-and-so, the tribe of so-and-so, etc.

﴿yufsidūna fī l-arḍi﴾ (Surah an-Naml, 48). Why, then, did He say after it: ﴿wa-lā yuṣlihūn﴾ (Surah an-Naml, 48)? They said: because a person may corrupt in one thing and reform in another, like those who mixed a righteous deed with another evil one, and for these it may be that Allah will turn in forgiveness to them.

As for these people, they were people of pure corruption who did not recognize righteousness. If they saw it, they set about corrupting it. It is as if they were insistent upon corruption. And corruption has people who profit from it, so they defend it and oppose, in its path, the people of reform and goodness, because these would deprive them of this profit.

We have said: the possessor of religion, morals and principles, in whatever public interest you see him, is disliked by this faction that profits from corruption. They attack him and pursue him with insinuation and slander, saying: "Hanbali," and perhaps mocking him, etc. Therefore, none stood against the messengers except this group that profits from corruption.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 49:

﴿They said: "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night..."﴾ (al-Naml 27:49). That is, the group (al-rahṭ).

﴿"...Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family..."﴾ (al-Naml 27:49). Consider this brazenness, lack of intelligence and shallowness of thought: they make a pact and swear by Allah that they will kill the Messenger of Allah. This is evidence of their stupidity, as though the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, were opening outlets through which their folly and lack of reason would appear.

The meaning of ﴿nubayyitannahu﴾ (we will attack him by night) (al-Naml 27:49) is: we will make him sleep at night. Al-baytutah (spending the night) is that a person ceases movement while asleep, then resumes movement upon waking in the morning. But these people want to make him spend the night in a sleep from which there is no rising. The meaning is: we will kill him.

Then, if the avengers of the blood come demanding his blood, ﴿"...we will say to his guardian..."﴾ (al-Naml 27:49), that is, the guardian of the blood from among his kinsmen and relatives, ﴿"...We did not witness the destruction of his family, and we are truthful."﴾ (al-Naml 27:49). That is: we did not witness the killing of his family, so much the more we did not witness his killing, and we know nothing of him.

This is what the people plotted against the Prophet of Allah Salih (peace be upon him). They thought that Allah would leave His Messenger unprotected, or would enable them to kill him. So they devised this scheme and did not neglect preparing a defense of themselves when questioned. This is their deceit and their planning.

Meaning of ﴿They plotted a plot... 50﴾ (An-Naml): that is, what they devised to kill the Prophet of Allah and His messenger to them. ﴿And We plotted a plot... 50﴾ (An-Naml). And there is a difference between the plotting of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And Allah is the best of planners 54﴾ (Al 'Imran), and the plotting of the disbelievers, ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people... 43﴾ (Fatir).

So, when you plot for good, it is not called plotting; rather, it is the nullification of the enemy's plotting. It is not permissible for you to let him scheme against you and plot against you while you do not move. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿And Allah is the best of planners 30﴾ (Al-Anfal), because they plot against a human being, while We plot to repel this evil and to support our Messenger and to save him from your scheming.

And "al-makr" (plotting) is derived from their saying: a "shajara mamkurah" (an intertwined tree). This refers to a tree of slender trunk that climbs, when its stems and branches wind around one another, so that you cannot distinguish one from another; each one is intertwined with and concealed within the other. Likewise, plotting is that you make something and conceal it from the opponent.

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and they do not perceive 50﴾ (An-Naml): that is, it is a plot that is carefully woven and firmly devised, such that the one plotted against does not know about it; otherwise it would not be plotting.

When we reflect on ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people... 43﴾ (Fatir) and ﴿And Allah is the best of planners 54﴾ (Al 'Imran), we know that plotting is not praised or blamed in itself; rather, the aim behind it is what matters, as in His saying, the Exalted, concerning suspicion: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion... 12﴾ (Al-Hujurat). For suspicion includes that which is good and that which is evil.

Now we hear a new expression that describes what goes on in society of the spread of plotting and ill-suspicion. They say: "Frankness is the plotting of the twentieth century." The one who schemes against people assumes that they are all scheming, so he does not believe their words, and he takes precautions against them even if they are telling the truth. Thus plotting and ill-suspicion have become the rule. If you are frank with the schemer, he does not believe you, and says to himself: "He is trying to deceive me, or to mislead me."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 27, verse 51:

Meaning: Consider what befell them when they plotted against the Prophet of Allah and agreed upon a night attack to kill him. It is related that when they entered upon him, a stone was thrown at each of them, one that they did not know where it came from, and they all perished. Allah had subjected to him angels who undertook his protection and his defence.

Or: Allah devised for him a stratagem by which he departed and went to Hadramawt, and there he, peace be upon him, died, and so it was named Hadramawt. Others said: rather, they went to wait for him at the foot of the mountain, and they hid behind a rock to ambush him, but the rock fell upon them and they all died.

In any case, Allah destroyed them by whichever of these means: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him...﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:31). They wanted to kill him and his family, so Allah destroyed them.

1 Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah sent the angels that night, and Salih's house was filled with them. The nine came to Salih's house brandishing their swords, and the angels stoned them to death with rocks; they saw the rocks but did not see who was throwing them. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5100).

2 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5102): "Salih went out with those who believed with him to Hadramawt, and when he entered it, Salih died, so it was named Hadramawt."

The words of the Exalted, ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of their wrongdoing﴾, are evidence that God destroyed them, so that not one of them remained, and their houses were left empty because of their wrongdoing. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, a lesson and an admonition, ﴿for a people who know﴾.

Opposite the destruction of the disbelievers:

﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾

So whoever among the people of Salih believed and was mindful of God, God, mighty and majestic, saved him from the punishment that descended upon his people, the Thamud.

The discussion here concludes the story of Thamud. When we compare the events mentioned here with what is related in Surah al-Shu'ara', we find new events that are not mentioned there, and nothing is mentioned here about the story of the she-camel that appears there, which indicates the complementary nature of the story's scenes across the different surahs.

(1) It is said: about four thousand men believed in Salih, while the rest had pustules break out on their bodies, according to the opinion of Muqatil and others, like chickpeas; on the first day they were red, then on the next day they became yellow, then on the third day they became black...

And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit an abomination while you see [it]?" (27:54)

"Lot" (لوطا) is in the accusative because it is the direct object; the implied sense is: "We sent Lot," as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah..."﴾ (an-Naml 27:45).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When he said to his people, "Do you commit an abomination while you see [it]?"﴾ (an-Naml 27:54), mentions the disease that had spread among them. In Surah ash-Shu'ara' He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Do you commit an abomination that no one in the worlds has preceded you in?﴾ (al-A'raf 7:80 as cited; the verse is in ash-Shu'ara' 26:165–166). Here He said: ﴿while you see [it]﴾ (an-Naml 27:54), meaning: you openly flaunt it and proclaim it, which shows that they had united upon it and approved of it, and that they no longer had any shame about practicing it.

Or the meaning may be: "while you see" what befell the perpetrators of corruption before you of the decrees of Allah against them.

This is an explanation and elaboration of the disease and the immorality that had spread among them. As for the meaning of His words ﴿Nay, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ (An-Naml 27:55): on its surface, it seems to contradict His words ﴿while you see﴾ (An-Naml 27:54). But the meaning of ﴿ignorant﴾ (tajhalun) here is not the opposite of knowledge; rather, ignorance (jahl) here means foolishness (safah).

Some people think that ignorance (jahl) is not knowing. No, illiteracy (ummiyyah) is not knowing; as for ignorance (jahl), it is knowing a matter that contradicts reality. For this reason, the unlettered person (ummi) is easier to persuade, because his mind is empty, whereas the ignorant person (jahil) holds a mistaken proposition, so it becomes necessary to remove from him the false proposition and then introduce the true one. Therefore, ignorance is, in this sense, more difficult for those who call to the truth (du'at) than illiteracy.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾

How strange is the matter of these people! Consider the reason they give for the expulsion and its ground: ﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾ (An-Naml). Glory be to Allah! When has purity become a sin and a crime that deserves its possessor being driven out of his land? It is a refrain we always hear from the people of falsehood in every age and place, whenever they attack the people of truth and seek to remove them from the arena so that their falsehood may have the field to itself.

Part of the justice of Allah the Exalted is that the proof of their condemnation and the corruption of their dispositions appears in their own speech. The word ﴿yatatahharun﴾ (Qur'an 27:56, An-Naml), which they uttered, means that they themselves are impure, disturbed by purity and by the good things that Allah has made lawful. It is as though the Exalted Truth places within their words openings through which they are condemned, so that they may pass judgment upon themselves by them.

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says:

﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife. We had decreed that she would be among those who remained behind.﴾

That is, among those destroyed along with her people. For she used to point out to her people the guests of Lot, so that they would come to them to commit the abomination with them. Therefore she was struck by the punishment just as her people were.

Meaning: how evil is this rain. Although the rain is left unspecified here, the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted, has clarified it in other verses, when He said: "of baked clay" (min tin), and "of hard-baked clay" (min sijjil), which is clay that has been fired until it becomes pottery. These stones were arranged and marked (musawwamah), which God made for them with precise calculation, so that each one of them had its own stone bearing his name, which would not miss him and strike anyone else.

(1) Sawama al-shay': he knew it by a sign. Al-sawma: the mark; al-sayma and al-sima' (with a kasra on the sin): the mark. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/337).

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 27, verse 59:

We know that Allah, exalted is He, is praised for blessings; but there is [the verse] ﴿All praise is for Allah...﴾ (al-Naml 27:59), which came after vengeance, punishment, and the seizing of the deniers.

They said: the address here is directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and in it there is an indication that the soldiers of Allah are the victors, that the final outcome is theirs, so that the Messenger of Allah may be reassured. Likewise, the purging of the earth of the corrupters is in it; and when the lands and the servants find rest from them, this is a blessing that deserves ﴿All praise is for Allah...﴾ (al-Naml 27:59).

In the destruction of the disbelievers and deniers there is also a lesson and a teaching for others, so that they do not become entangled in the causes of destruction. This is another blessing that deserves praise.

Therefore our Lord, blessed and exalted, has commanded us to praise Him if we see good descend upon the righteous, or evil fall upon the wicked. So the meaning of ﴿Say: All praise is for Allah...﴾ (al-Naml 27:59) is that the messengers prevailed and triumphed, and the corrupters were routed and defeated.

Do you not see the words of the people of Paradise:
﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, abiding eternally." And they will say, "All praise is for Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has made us inherit the land, to settle in Paradise wherever we will..."﴾ (al-Zumar 39:73–74)

Likewise, when we see the wicked man whose evil has spread and whose corruption has multiplied, when there descends upon him what he deserves of the punishment of Allah in full, at the moment we hear his news we say: "All praise is for Allah." Thus, by an involuntary process, everyone's tongues move to praise at the descent of a blessing upon its people and a punishment upon one who deserves it.

He, exalted is He, says about the people of evil and corruption:
﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship that they might humble themselves. So why did they not humble themselves when Our punishment came to them? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they had been doing. And when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of every [good] thing until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were [then] in despair. So the last remnant of the wrongdoing people was eliminated. And all praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (al-An'am 6:42–45)

So after Allah cut off the remnant of the wrongdoers, He said: "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds." Here we note the difference between fataha laka and fataha 'alayka. Fataha laka means: opened in your favour, as in ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory﴾ (al-Fath 48:1).

As for fataha 'alayhim, it means: with evil, the particle 'alayhim being a figurative indication against them. So the meaning of ﴿We opened to them the gates of every [good] thing...﴾ (al-An'am 6:44) is that He gave them good in order to destroy them by it, while they were in a state of blessing and standing, until when Allah seized them, His seizing was painful and severe.

In the story of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿So when you and those with you are settled upon the ship, say, "All praise is for Allah, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:28)

So he praised Allah here for two matters: "All praise is for Allah" because He drowned the disbelieving wrongdoers and rid us of them, and "All praise is for Allah" because He saved the believers.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen...﴾ (al-Naml 27:59). They are the believers whom Allah helped and to whom He gave the final outcome, and the peace upon them after what they encountered of the obstinacy and stubbornness of the disbelievers. So "All praise is for Allah who destroyed the corrupters and brought peace upon the guided."

Then the Truth, exalted is He, poses a question, presenting it in the form of an interrogation, so that it may be more striking to the soul than mere statement: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate [with Him]?﴾ (al-Naml 27:59).

Had the verse said: "Say: All praise is for Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen, because Allah is better and what they associate [with Him] is evil," the discourse would have been informative, and information in itself, regardless of its speaker, admits of truth or falsehood.

But when this matter is presented in the form of a question, it makes your addressee the one who utters it, as if one of your friends denied your favour and your kindness towards him; instead of you informing him, "I did for you such-and-such," you leave him to inform, and you say: "Did I not do for you such-and-such?" No one says this except one who is confident and certain that the answer will be in his favour.

So the meaning of ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate [with Him]?﴾ (al-Naml 27:59) is: "Tell us yourselves, and we accept your judgment, after what you have seen and heard of this story: is Allah better, or those who associate others with Him?" The answer must be: Allah is better. Therefore, when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was moved by it and hastened to answer: "Rather, Allah is better and more enduring, more majestic and more generous."(3)

This shows that being moved by the Qur'an is obligatory, and we mean being moved by its meanings, not being moved by the sound and melodies like what we hear from those "dhikira" (noisy reciters) who encourage the reciters with shouting and clamour that does not befit the majesty of the verses, and who, despite that, do not understand the meanings nor are affected by them, to the point that one of them hears verses of punishment and says at the top of his voice: "O Allah, increase us!"

The scribes among the Companions were moved by the verses in meaning, to the extent that one of them would complete a verse and conclude it with what suits it before it was dictated to him. Why? Because they understood from Allah and were affected by the meaning, which indicates that the Qur'an came in accordance with sound human nature.
